course.title: English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric
course.description: Take sentences apart and rebuild them, test arguments, scan Shakespeare and read Austen the way a critic does.
course.audience: A fluent adult reader who wants to write with precision and read literature critically. No grammar course or literary training is assumed; school terms are defined when they appear.

paragraphs: When Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863 he said “we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground”, where five words, “we cannot dedicate this ground”, would have carried the same fact, yet it is the longer sentence that people remember. It repeats its opening three times, brings in a new verb each time and holds back the thing being spoken of until the very end, and each of those choices is something we can point to on the page and give a name to.

Rhetoric, the study of how speech and writing persuade, is the old name for thinking about choices like these, and close reading is the same work done from the reader's side. A writer decides which word leads a sentence, which reasons to state and which to leave the reader to supply, where the beats fall in a line of verse and who tells a story, and each decision changes what the reader understands and how far they are moved. Once we can see the decisions we can say why a speech persuades or why a line stays in the memory, and we can make the same decisions on purpose in our own writing, which is the difference between feeling that a paragraph falls flat and knowing how to mend it.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the verb and its subject in a line of verse, even when the words are shuffled.
You'll be able to join two clauses with the mark that says what you mean.
You'll be able to rewrite a passive or padded sentence so that the actor leads and every word counts.
You'll be able to split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, and say where it can be attacked.
You'll be able to scan a line of pentameter and say who is telling a story and how far to trust them.

lead.text: How do you find the verb in a sentence? The usual answer, that it is the word for an action, fails quickly: in “She is tired” nothing is happening, and yet “is” is the verb, while a noun like “collapse” names an action without being a verb at all. A better test is to move the whole sentence to another time and watch **which word has to change**. Take “She opens the window” and say it about yesterday, and you get “She opened the window”, where every word has stayed as it was except *one*.

The word that moved is the one that carries the time of the sentence, and we call it the **finite verb**, finite in the sense of *limited*, because the time (and, in a word like “opens”, the person acting) pins down its form. Some forms of a verb never change with the time, “to open” and “opening” for example, and the figure shows them standing still while the finite verb moves. Those forms cannot be the verb of a sentence on their own, which is why the finite verb is the one to look for.

afterFigure.text: The test asks only which word changes with the time, so it works on any sentence in prose or in verse, *whatever* order the words come in. It is the first thing to try on a line you cannot make sense of.

reveal.text: Said about the past, the line becomes “And every fair from fair sometime declined”, and nothing else moves. The verb comes last, after everything that says what declines and when, so its position is no clue at all. Poets move words about freely, but the time test does not care where the words stand.

lead.text: Once you have the [[finite verb|The word that changes when a sentence moves to another time. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]], ask who or what does it, or is it. In “The old dog barked loudly at dusk”, the answer to “who barked?” is the old dog, and we call that the **subject**. A finite verb together with its subject makes a **clause**, the smallest group of words that says something complete, and everything else in the sentence hangs from that pair. Here “loudly” and “at dusk” add how and when; words that add detail in this way are **modifiers**, and you can take them away without breaking the clause.

Now switch the figure to Shakespeare's line. The subject is “every fair”, the thing that declines, and the verb is “declines”, but “from fair” and “sometime” have been put between them. They are modifiers, and the poet's placing of them makes the line harder to read without changing its core.

afterFigure.text: This is why the *pair* matters more than the *order*. A writer can move modifiers around for rhythm or emphasis, but **the subject and its finite verb stay joined**, and you can always find them by asking who or what the verb is about.

lead.text: Many clauses go on past the verb. Compare “The wind rattled the shutters” with “The wind was cold”. In the first, the shutters are what the wind acts on, and the word for whatever receives the action is the **object**. In the second, “was” describes no action at all; it links the wind to a description, and the word that completes the link is a **complement**. Verbs that do this job, such as “was”, “seems” and “became”, are called **linking verbs**.
So the question to ask is about the verb: does something *receive* its action, or does the verb only say what the subject *is* or is like? The figure lets you set the two clauses side by side.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the job a word does depends on the verb in front of it, and not on the kind of word it is. “Cold” is an adjective, a word that describes a noun, but a noun can be a complement as well: in “She became a doctor”, “a doctor” describes her. And when an object or complement runs to several words, one noun in it is the **head noun**, the word the others describe, as the next example shows.

steps.headline: Is the last word of “The storm was fierce” an object or a complement?

lead.text: Take two clauses that look almost alike, “The storm shook the roof” and “The storm was fierce”, and put the question about the verb to each in turn.

workedSteps.text: In the first clause the verb is “shook”. Asking what the storm shook gives “the roof”, so the roof *receives* the action and is the [[object|The word or phrase that receives the verb's action. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]].
In the second clause the verb is “was”, and asking what the storm was gives “fierce”. *Nothing* is being done to anything here, so the word cannot be an object.
That leaves one possibility, and the next question is what “fierce” does for the storm.

steps.headline: Find the head of an object that has several words

lead.text: An object can be one word or a whole phrase, and in a phrase one word carries the meaning while the rest *describe* it. Take Sonnet 18, line 3, “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

reveal.text: Remove the describing words and the clause still works: the winds shake the buds. Remove “buds” instead and nothing is left for “darling” and “of May” to describe.

workedSteps.text: The finite verb is “do shake”, which in the past would be “did shake”, and its subject is “rough winds”.
What is shaken is the phrase “the darling buds of May”, so the whole phrase is the object.
The phrase has a head noun, the one word that “darling” and “of May” both describe.

lead.text: So far every clause we have looked at could be a sentence by itself, but that is not always so. In “We stayed inside because it was raining”, both “we stayed inside” and “it was raining” have a subject and a finite verb, and so both are clauses, yet **only the first makes sense alone**. The second begins with “because”, a word that makes the clause lean on another one for its meaning. A clause that can stand alone is an **independent clause**, a clause that cannot is a **dependent clause**, and the little word that makes it dependent is a **subordinator**. Others you will meet are “when”, “since”, “although” and “which”.

Switch the figure to its second view and you will see the opposite case, “The tide came in and the beach vanished”, where “and” joins two clauses that could each be a sentence. “And” joins them without making either depend on the other.

afterFigure.text: A dependent clause usually answers a question about its partner: why did we stay inside? because it was raining. That is the sense in which it *depends* on the other clause, and it is why a dependent clause on its own feels unfinished.

reveal.text: Take “if” away and “snow be white” is a statement that could stand on its own. With it, the clause only sets up a condition and leaves “her breasts are dun” to answer it.

lead.text: Every clause has exactly one finite verb, so **counting finite verbs counts clauses**, provided you count the *right* words. Compare “Anna decided to leave when she saw the rain” with “Walking home, Mia hummed a tune”. In the first, “decided” and “saw” are finite, since in the present they would become “decides” and “sees”, whereas “to leave” is an **infinitive**, a verb form that stays the same whatever the time. In the second, “walking” is a **participle**, another form that does not move with the time, so “hummed” is the only finite verb and the sentence holds one clause.

Two cautions help when you count in a real text. A verb phrase such as “do shake” or “was raining” counts once, because the helping word carries the time and the whole phrase acts as one verb. And when you doubt a candidate, run the time test on it, since a word that cannot change with the time cannot be a finite verb.

reveal.text: Each of the three has its own subject: “love”, “which” (standing for love) and “it”. Once the clauses are counted separately, the line stops looking like one long tangle.

blocks.text: Here is a line from Shakespeare's Sonnet 18: “And every fair from fair sometime declines.” Read it twice and you may feel you understand it without being able to say *how*, because the words come in an order nobody would use in conversation. Which word says what happens, and which says to whom, or to what, it happens?

There is a reliable way to find out, and it does not depend on word order or on how a line sounds. Every sentence is built around a small core, a verb and the person or thing it is about, and once you can find that core you can read a tangled line of verse, or a tangled sentence of your own, by working outwards from it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the finite verb and its subject in a line of verse, tell an object from a complement, and say whether a clause can stand alone.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later skill in this course, from punctuating a sentence to scanning a line of verse, begins with finding where one clause ends and the next begins.

recap.keyIdea: A clause is a finite verb with its subject; what follows the verb is an object or a complement, and a clause that cannot stand alone is dependent.

blocks.text: To read a sentence, find the **finite verb** by moving the sentence to another time and seeing which word has to change, then ask who or what it is about to find the subject. After the verb comes an *object* if something receives the action and a *complement* if the verb only links the subject to a description.

A clause that begins with a subordinator such as “if” or “because” is dependent, since it cannot stand alone, and because every clause has exactly one finite verb you can count clauses by counting finite verbs, leaving out infinitives and participles.

lessons.title: Joining two clauses

lead.text: Take “The shop closed” and “we went home”. Each is an [[independent clause|A clause that can stand alone as a sentence. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]], so each could end with a full stop, and a full stop keeps them as two sentences while saying nothing about how they connect. If you want them in one sentence, the usual way is a comma followed by a **coordinating conjunction**, one of the seven words *for, and, nor, but, or, yet* and *so*, and the conjunction does something useful: **it names the relation**. “The shop closed, so we went home” tells the reader that the closing was the reason.

The comma without the conjunction is where writers go wrong. “The shop closed, we went home” puts two independent clauses side by side with a comma between them, and a comma is *too light* to hold them together, so the reader cannot tell where one thought ends and the next begins. Editors call this a **comma splice**. Writers have long used it for effect, and Frederick Douglass wrote “You may rejoice, I must mourn” in 1852, but modern edited prose treats it as an error, so you need to know how to repair it.

afterFigure.text: The figure puts two repairs of the same pair side by side. The full stop separates the thoughts and leaves the connection unsaid, whereas the comma with “so” keeps them in one sentence and says *outright* that one led to the other.

reveal.text: The comma sits between two complete clauses, and nothing else is there to join them. The word comes from joining two lengths of rope or film end to end, and a comma alone makes that kind of weak join.

lead.text: The semicolon is the mark that lets two [[independent clauses|A clause that can stand alone as a sentence. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]] share a sentence *without* saying how they are related. In “The hall emptied; the street filled”, the reader sees the connection for themselves (people left the hall and went into the street), because the semicolon tells them only that the two clauses belong together. That is why it needs no conjunction after it: it **already links two full clauses as one thought**, and a conjunction after it would do the mark's work a second time.

A semicolon can also show that something has been left out. When the second clause would repeat the verb of the first, a writer may drop it and let the reader carry the verb across, as in “Alice chose tea; Ben, coffee; Carol, juice.” The missing “chose” is understood, and the name for leaving out an understood word is **ellipsis**. The semicolon sits where the gap falls, and it keeps the three clauses reading as a single list of choices.

afterFigure.text: Douglass uses exactly this pattern in the Rochester speech, with a good deal more at stake than a choice of drinks, and the next example takes it apart.

steps.headline: Repair the splice “The lamp flickered, the room went dark”

lead.text: The sentence has two independent clauses and only a comma between them, so it is a [[comma splice|Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. There are two natural repairs, and they differ in how much they say.

workedSteps.text: Repair one is a semicolon: “The lamp flickered; the room went dark.” Each side is a *complete* clause, and the reader is left to see how the two events connect.
Repair two keeps the comma and adds one of the seven coordinating conjunctions, and which of them you choose depends on what you mean to say.
So the question to settle is which repair says outright that the flicker caused the dark.

steps.headline: Find the word Douglass left out

lead.text: Douglass, speaking in Rochester on 5 July 1852, strings three clauses together with semicolons: “To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.” Only the first has a verb that you can see.

reveal.text: Your boasted liberty *is* an unholy license, and your national greatness *is* swelling vanity. With only commas the three clauses would blur into a list, whereas the semicolons mark the places where the same verb is understood.

workedSteps.text: The first clause is complete: “your celebration is a sham”, with “to him” as a modifier.
The second, “your boasted liberty, an unholy license”, and the third, “your national greatness, swelling vanity”, have a subject and a complement but no finite verb of their own.
The reader supplies the missing verb from the first clause, and the question is which word that is.

lead.text: A colon makes a promise. When you write “The reason was simple: the bridge was closed”, the words before the colon raise an expectation and the clause after it satisfies the expectation, so the second clause *explains* the first. For the promise to work, **whatever stands before the colon must be a complete clause** that could be a sentence on its own, and that is the one rule to take away.

Shakespeare gives a clean example in Sonnet 18. The second line makes a claim, “Thou art more lovely and more temperate”, and ends with a colon, and the third line supplies the evidence: “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May.” The colon tells us that the winds are the reason the beloved is the more temperate, which a semicolon would have left us to *guess*.

afterFigure.text: Compare it with the semicolon from the last screen. A semicolon says only that the two thoughts belong together, but a colon says in which *direction* the explanation runs, from the clause before it to the clause after.

reveal.text: The colon belongs after a clause that could end a sentence. Anything less, and the mark cuts a clause in half instead of promising an explanation.

lead.text: You now have several ways to join two clauses, and they differ in how much they say. A conjunction names the relation outright (*so* for a result, *but* for a contrast, *and* for an addition), a semicolon says only that the thoughts belong together, and a colon says that the second explains the first. A dash is the most abrupt of them: it breaks the sentence to add something, and writers use it for emphasis, as Lincoln does at Gettysburg in 1863: “we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground.”

So the way to choose is to **decide what you want the reader to know about the relation**. The figure joins the same two clauses about a river and a road in three ways, each of which tells the reader something different.

afterFigure.text: Notice that no mark is better than the others in general. The conjunction is the clearest when the relation matters, and the semicolon is right when the relation is obvious and you want the sentence to move quickly.

lead.text: Marks of punctuation do not make clauses; *verbs* do. Whatever stands between the clauses, whether a semicolon, a colon or a comma with a conjunction, you count an independent clause each time you find **a subject with a finite verb that could stand alone**. “The ferry was cancelled; the crowd waited; the next boat was due at noon” has three, even though no conjunction appears.

The count changes when a clause opens with a [[subordinator|A word such as because, if or when that makes a clause depend on another. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]]. In “The ferry was cancelled because the wind rose; the crowd waited”, the clause beginning with “because” is dependent, so there are two independent clauses and one that leans on the first. Use the same habit as in the last lesson, and test each candidate by asking whether it could be a sentence by itself.

reveal.text: Lincoln in the figure's second view shows another way: dashes join his three clauses with no conjunction at all, and the repeated “we can not” makes the series read as one long insistence.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to say that you waited at the stop and that the bus never came. Those are two complete thoughts, and you could set them side by side with a comma, a semicolon or a colon and the sentence would look tidy each time. The marks are not interchangeable, though, because each tells the reader something *different* about how the second thought relates to the first, and one of them is an error.

Only the comma is an error here, and the reason is worth knowing, because it shows what a mark between two clauses is for. Each of the other marks says something about how the second thought stands to the first, so choosing a mark means choosing what the reader will take the connection to be, and once you know what each one says you can join any two clauses so that the sentence means exactly what you intend.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to repair a comma splice and choose the mark, a semicolon, a colon, a dash or a conjunction, that says what you mean about how two clauses relate.
intro.whyItMatters: A wrongly chosen mark either misleads the reader about how two thoughts connect or leaves them unable to see where one thought ends.

recap.keyIdea: Join two independent clauses with a mark that says what you mean: a comma alone is a splice, a conjunction names the relation, a semicolon leaves it to the reader, and a colon promises an explanation.

blocks.text: A **comma splice** joins two independent clauses with only a comma, and you repair it with a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma and a coordinating conjunction that names the relation. A semicolon tells the reader that two complete clauses belong together, and it can stand where a verb has been left out, while a colon must follow a complete clause and promises that what comes next explains it.
Whatever mark you use, you count clauses by their verbs, so each subject with a finite verb that could stand alone is one independent clause.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at which word leads a sentence, and why putting the actor first often makes a sentence shorter and clearer.

lessons.title: Actors and actions

lead.text: In “The dog ate the sandwich”, the subject is the dog, and it is the dog that does the eating. When the subject performs the action in this way, the sentence is in the **active voice**. Now turn the sentence round: “The sandwich was eaten by the dog.” The facts are the same, but the sandwich has moved into the subject position, the verb has become “was eaten”, and the dog has been pushed to the end behind the word “by”. This is the **passive voice**, in which the subject *receives* the action.

The passive is built from a form of “be” and the [[participle|A verb form that does not move with the time, such as “walking” or “eaten”. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]], and it costs words: “ate” has become “was eaten”, and “by” has had to be added. The figure lets you switch each sentence between its two versions, so you can watch the actor travel from the front to the back.

afterFigure.text: Neither version is *wrong*. The active starts from the doer, which is where readers usually expect to start, and the passive starts from the thing affected, which is sometimes the thing you want to talk about. The trouble begins when **the passive is used out of habit** rather than for a reason.

lead.text: The passive has a second feature that matters even more than its length, which is that **the “by” phrase is optional**. “The office was closed by the manager” can lose its ending and become “The office was closed”, a complete and grammatical sentence in which *nobody* has closed anything. The one who performs the action is called the **agent**, and a passive that leaves the agent out is an **agentless passive**.

There are honest reasons to leave the agent out. It may be unknown (“The shop was broken into overnight”), or obvious from context, or beside the point (“The hall was painted last summer”). But the agentless passive also lets a writer say that something happened without saying who did it, which is why “mistakes were made” has become the stock phrase for admitting a fault without owning it.

afterFigure.text: So the question to ask of any passive is whether **the reader needs to know who acted**. If they do, the agent belongs in the sentence, and the simplest way to put it there is to make it the subject.

steps.headline: Rewrite “The report was approved by the director in May”

lead.text: The sentence is passive, and the method is to find the *agent*, make it the *subject*, and turn the verb back into a plain one.

workedSteps.text: First, find who did the approving. A passive moves the agent out of the subject, and when it names the agent at all it puts it in a phrase of its own later in the sentence.
So the thing to settle is which phrase of the sentence holds the agent.
Next, make the director the subject and turn “was approved” back into the plain past verb “approved”, so that the report becomes its object.
Last, keep the modifier and drop “by”, which has no work left to do: “The director approved the report in May.” Nine words have become seven.

steps.headline: Put the finance office back in the subject

lead.text: The sentence is “Mistakes were made by the finance office”, which is the agentless passive's favourite sentence with its agent put back in.

reveal.text: “The finance office made mistakes.” The sentence now says who made them, and it is two words *shorter*, five against seven.

workedSteps.text: Its subject is “mistakes”, the thing acted on, and its verb is “were made”.
The “by” phrase holds the agent, and moving the agent to the front will turn the verb back into “made”.
In the active sentence, which words are the subject?

lead.text: Look at “The board gave approval to the plan”. The action is approving, but the word for it is a noun, “approval”, and the verb the sentence is left with, “gave”, does nothing except carry that noun along. Turning a verb into a noun in this way is called **nominalisation**, and it leaves the action hidden in a noun with a weak verb such as “make”, “give” or “have” standing in for it. Say **the action as a verb** and the sentence comes back to life: “The board approved the plan”, which has three words fewer.

The figure shows two examples of the same repair, in which the phrase that hides the verb is replaced by the verb itself. Notice that the actor never moves in these examples; it is the *action* that comes out of hiding.

afterFigure.text: Nominalisations are common in official writing because nouns sound solemn, and that is also why they pile up with [[passives|Sentences whose subject receives the action. Met earlier in this lesson.]]: “The approval of the plan was given by the board” has both faults at once, and says nothing that “The board approved the plan” does not say *better*.

lead.text: Once the actor leads and the action is a verb, a third kind of fault is easier to see: words that add length and no meaning. Some are frames, like “It is a fact that” in front of “the bakery opens at nine”; the reader will take the statement as a fact unless you tell them otherwise, so the frame can go. Others repeat a meaning the sentence already holds, as “free” does in “free gift”, or are long ways of saying a short thing, as “at this point in time” is for “now”. We can call such words **padding**.
The test for padding is to **take the words out and see whether the sentence loses anything**. If it does not, they were padding, and if it does, they were *doing work*.

A real sentence often needs more than one edit, and the *order* matters. Take “The courier completed the delivery of the parcels on Monday, as a matter of fact.” The actor is already in the subject, so look for a buried verb and then for padding. “Completed the delivery of” hides the verb “delivered”, and “as a matter of fact” is a frame that has drifted to the end of the sentence.

Make both edits and fifteen words become seven: “The courier delivered the parcels on Monday.” The figure shows the two edits one at a time, and the order is a good habit: **restore the actor, unbury the verb, and only then cut** what is left over, because cutting first can make you throw away words you would have *needed*.

segments.text: The courier delivered the parcels on Monday,

reveal.text: The figure's second view shows the same habit on another sentence: “At this point in time the committee is in agreement that the plan is a good one” becomes “Now the committee agrees that the plan is good.”

lessons.orientation: Move actors into subjects and actions into verbs. Switch between active and passive, unbury nominalisations and count the words a revision saves.

blocks.text: Compare two ways of reporting the same broken window: “Sam broke the window” and “The window was broken by Sam.” The facts are identical, yet most readers find the first *quicker*, and writing guides have long told us to prefer it. Is the advice sound, and when would the longer version be the better choice?

The answer depends on a decision that every sentence makes, which is who comes first. A sentence can lead with the one who acts or with the one acted on, and the choice changes what the reader notices, how many words you need, and whether anyone can be held responsible.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the actor in the subject and the action in the verb, switch between active and passive, and count the words a revision saves.
intro.whyItMatters: Sentences that name who does what are shorter and clearer, and they are harder to use to dodge responsibility.

recap.keyIdea: Clear sentences put the actor in the subject and the action in a verb, and they cut whatever adds length without adding meaning.

blocks.text: A sentence is **active** when its subject performs the action and **passive** when its subject receives it, and the passive can leave the agent out altogether. A **nominalisation** hides an action in a noun, so the verb you are left with has nothing to do, and unburying it usually saves several words.
When you revise, restore the actor first, then unbury the verb, then cut the padding, and read the result aloud to make sure nothing the reader needs has gone.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn from sentences to arguments, and take one apart into the claim it makes, the grounds it offers and the rule that links them.

lessons.title: Claim, grounds and warrant

lead.text: Every argument has at least two parts. The **claim** is the statement the arguer wants you to accept, and the **grounds** are the facts or reasons offered to support it. A coach who says “Pick Mia for the team: she scored twenty goals this season” makes the claim in the first half of the sentence, “pick Mia”, and gives the grounds in the second. Position tells you *nothing*, since “Every light in the house is on, so someone is at home” puts the grounds first.

To find the claim, **ask which statement the others are there to support**, and the answer is the claim whichever place it occupies. The figure sets out two arguments with their parts labelled, and you can compare how the grounds and the claim relate in each.

afterFigure.text: The model we are building is Stephen Toulmin's, from his book *The Uses of Argument* (1958), and it has six parts. We start with the two that nearly every argument states aloud, and the rest of the lesson adds the ones that usually go unsaid.

statements.text: Pick Mia for the team.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Every light in the house is on.
Someone is at home.

reveal.text: The claim comes in the middle of the three statements here, between a fact and a general rule, which is why position is no guide. The figure's second view shows the argument from the letter we started with.

statements.text: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.
The library should open on Sundays.
Nearly every other library in the county opens on Sundays.
A library should do what most libraries in its county do.

lead.text: Look again at the coach. Twenty goals is a fact, and “pick Mia” is a decision, and nothing in the first forces the second. What connects them is a rule that nobody says aloud: players who score a lot help a team. **Without that rule the grounds prove nothing**, and with it they point straight at the claim. Toulmin called such a rule the **warrant**, borrowing the legal sense of a document that gives authority to act, because it is what *authorises* the step from the grounds to the claim.

The lights work in the same way. “Every light is on” supports “someone is at home” only because we assume that people switch lights on when they are in. Notice the difference in kind: the grounds are a *particular* fact, which you can check by looking, whereas the warrant is a *general* rule about how the world works.

afterFigure.text: Warrants are usually left unstated, because they seem obvious to the person who holds them, and so the skill is to *say them aloud*. When you can state the warrant of an argument, you can ask whether it is true, and that is where a good reply begins.

statements.text: Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Pick Mia for the team.
Players who score a lot help a team.
Every light in the house is on.
Someone is at home.
People switch lights on when they are in.

steps.headline: Take apart “It will rain tomorrow, because the forecast says so”

lead.text: The method for any argument is the same: find the claim, find the grounds, and then ask **what rule would have to be true for the grounds to count**.

workedSteps.text: The claim is “It will rain tomorrow”, because it is what the speaker wants you to accept and the other statement is there to support it.
The grounds are “the forecast says rain”, a particular fact that you could check by looking up the forecast.
Now ask what you would have to believe for that fact to be a reason at all.

Once the [[warrant|The usually unstated rule that links grounds to claim. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is out in the open, you can test it. Forecasts are right more often than not, but *not always*, and that is exactly the point where a sceptic would press.

steps.headline: Name the rule behind the fingerprints

lead.text: Here is an argument from a courtroom, with one of its parts left unstated.

reveal.text: The rule is “Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it”, and Toulmin's word for it is the warrant. The same figure's second view does the job for a café: “It is Saturday lunchtime” supports “The café will be busy” only because cafés are busy then.

workedSteps.text: The grounds are “The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife”, a fact that the court can check.
The claim is “The defendant handled the knife”, which is what the prosecution wants the jury to accept.
Between them stands an unstated rule, and the question is what Toulmin called it.

statements.text: The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
It is Saturday lunchtime.
The café will be busy.
Cafés are busy at Saturday lunchtime.

lead.text: Because the warrant carries the step from the grounds to the claim, it is **where a clever opponent presses**. A defence lawyer in the knife case will rarely deny that the fingerprints are there, since that is a fact and the prosecution can show it. What the lawyer disputes is the *rule*, and says that fingerprints show a touch at some time, which is not the same as holding the knife during the crime.

That gives you a practical test. Grounds are facts, and you attack them by checking whether they are true; warrants are principles, and you attack them by asking whether they hold in this case. The figure marks the grounds as undisputed and the warrant as the weak point.

afterFigure.text: Notice that attacking the warrant does not show the claim is false. It shows only that this argument has not established it, which is a smaller and *more honest* conclusion.

lead.text: Real arguments rarely claim certainty, and Toulmin gave two parts to the ways they hedge. A **qualifier** is a word or phrase such as “very likely” or “in most cases” that states how strongly the claim is made. A **rebuttal** states a condition under which the claim would fail, and it is usually introduced by “unless”. In “In most cases the ferry will sail on time, unless fog closes the harbour”, the qualifier is “in most cases”, and the rebuttal is “unless fog closes the harbour”.

It can seem that hedging weakens an argument, but a claim that admits its limits is *easier to believe*, because it shows that the arguer has thought about how it could be wrong. The figure shows the ferry and the coach again with their limits added.

afterFigure.text: Qualifier and rebuttal do different work. The qualifier adjusts the strength of the claim itself, and the rebuttal names the circumstance that would defeat it, so a claim can have one, both or neither.

statements.text: The harbour has been clear all week.
In most cases,
The ferry will sail on time.
Unless fog closes the harbour.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Very likely,
Mia will help the team.
Unless an injury keeps her out.
Harriet leads every poll by eight points.
Probably.
Harriet will win the election.
Unless rain keeps her supporters at home.
The air pressure is falling fast.
Very likely.
It will rain tomorrow.
Unless the front stalls over the coast.

lead.text: A warrant is itself a claim, and a sceptic may ask why we should accept it. The support we give it is called **backing**, and it is different from grounds, which support the *claim* rather than the *rule*. Take a doctor who says that a patient should take an antibiotic because the infection is bacterial. The warrant is that antibiotics treat bacterial infections, and the backing is the clinical trials that show they do.

In the knife case the backing would be forensic studies showing that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact. With backing in place, the warrant stops being an assumption and becomes a conclusion of its own, supported by evidence.

afterFigure.text: You will not always find backing in an argument, and often it would take too long to state. But whenever a warrant is doubtful, the next question to ask is what supports it.

statements.text: The infection is bacterial.
Almost certainly,
The patient should take an antibiotic.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
Clinical trials show that antibiotics clear bacterial infections.
Unless the patient is allergic.
The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
Forensic studies show that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact.

reveal.text: The figure's second view runs the same pattern on a different subject: street trees need shade to be worth planting, and the roots may damage pipes, which is the rebuttal.

Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
The price should return to its old level.
Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
The council should plant trees on Gale Street.
Gale Street is hotter in summer than streets that have trees.
Shade lowers the temperature of a street.
Unless the roots would damage the pipes below.

lessons.orientation: Take an argument apart with Toulmin's model: the claim and the grounds offered for it, the warrant that links them, the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.

blocks.text: A letter to a local paper says: “The library should open on Sundays. Nearly every other library in the county does.” Is that a good argument? Most of us feel that something is thin about it without being able to say where, and a *feeling* is not much use if you want to answer the letter, or to write a better one yourself.

The reason is that an argument is made of parts that do different jobs, and one of the parts is almost never written down. The parts can be named using the model that the philosopher Stephen Toulmin set out in *The Uses of Argument* (1958), so that you can see which part is carrying the weight and where an opponent would press.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, spot its qualifier and rebuttal, and say where it can be attacked.
intro.whyItMatters: Once you can name the parts of an argument you can say exactly what is wrong with a weak one, and build a stronger one yourself.

recap.keyIdea: Every argument has a claim and grounds, a warrant that links them, and often a qualifier, a rebuttal and backing; the warrant is usually unstated and is where it is most easily attacked.

blocks.text: An argument rests on a **claim** and the **grounds** offered for it, and between them stands a **warrant**, a general rule that is usually unstated and that makes the step from the grounds to the claim legitimate. Because it carries the weight, the warrant is where an argument is most easily attacked.

The qualifier says how strongly the claim is made, the rebuttal says when it would fail, and the backing is the evidence that supports the warrant itself, so naming the parts tells you what to ask of any argument you meet.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn from the structure of an argument to the ways speakers persuade, following four appeals through speeches by Douglass and Lincoln.

lessons.title: Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos

lead.text: More than two thousand years ago Aristotle, in his *Rhetoric*, asked what a speaker can do to persuade, and found that the speech itself offers three means. The first is the audience's sense of the speaker, which he called **ethos**, the Greek word for character and the root of our word *ethics*: an audience believes a speaker it trusts. The second is the feeling the speech stirs, which he called **pathos**, the root of *sympathy*: an audience is moved to act when it is moved to feel. The third is the reasoning, which he called **logos**, a word that means both *word* and *reason*: an audience is persuaded when the case makes sense.

Take a meeting about a bus route. A speaker who opens “I have ridden the number 9 to work for thirty years” is building ethos, because she has told you why you should listen to her. “Picture your own child waiting at the school gate in the dark” is pathos, and “Three of the last five buses ran late and the timetable has not changed, so it will run late again” is logos. The figure marks all three in two invented examples.

afterFigure.text: In practice a good speech uses all three at once, and a single sentence can do more than one job, but one of them is usually doing *most* of the work. Learning to say which one is the first step in analysing a speech.

lead.text: Now consider an audience that has every reason to be suspicious of the speaker's argument. On 5 July 1852, in Rochester, New York, Frederick Douglass stood before people who had gathered to mark American independence. He had escaped from slavery in 1838 and was by then one of the best-known speakers in the country, and he did not begin by attacking his hearers. He began by telling them **where he stood**: “I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!” (the *pale* is a boundary, as in “beyond the pale”). A little later he says, “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn.”

These lines draw on his own standing, the authority of a man who had lived under the system he was about to condemn. Notice how this works *against* the occasion: an audience that has come to celebrate cannot easily set aside the word of someone whose experience of the nation was so different from their own.

spans.text: I am not included within the pale of this glorious anniversary!
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.
You may rejoice, I must mourn.
As chair of this society for twelve years, I have signed every one of its accounts.

steps.headline: Name the appeal in “As a lifelong farmer, I can tell you this drought is different”

lead.text: To name the appeal in any sentence, ask **what it does to the audience**: does it make them *trust* the speaker, *feel* something, or *follow a reason*?

workedSteps.text: First ask what the opening clause is about, the drought or the person speaking. It is about the *speaker*, who is telling us how long she has worked the land.
Next ask whether it gives a reason or paints a picture. It does neither, because it offers no evidence about the drought and asks us to imagine nothing.
What is left is the job the clause does for the speaker, and the question is what that job is.

steps.headline: Name the appeal in Douglass's two sunlights

lead.text: A few sentences after the line we have just read, Douglass says: “The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.”

reveal.text: It is pathos. The earlier line, “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine”, rests on his *standing*; this one rests on a *picture*. Douglass moves from one appeal to the other within a few sentences, and the second prepares the audience to accept what the first has claimed.

workedSteps.text: The sentence is built on one image, sunlight, and it means life and healing for one half of the sentence and the whip for the other.
It names no credentials and gives no premise from which a conclusion follows. What it does is set a *picture* of comfort next to a picture of suffering.
That rules out two of the three appeals, and the question is which one is left.

spans.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.
This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.

lead.text: Eleven years later, on 19 November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke for a few minutes at the dedication of a cemetery for the soldiers who had died at Gettysburg. He began in an old-fashioned way, with a count of years rather than a date: “Four score and seven years ago.” A score is twenty, so four score is eighty, and four score and seven is **eighty-seven**. The figure builds the phrase one block at a time, on a scale counted back from the day he spoke.

Counting back that far takes us to one particular year, and that year is the point of the opening. Lincoln is about to claim that the nation began with a *proposition*, and the date he has chosen sends his hearers back to the document where the proposition was first made.

reveal.text: Lincoln's phrase points to the year the Declaration of Independence was adopted, and the next sentence of the figure shows what he does with that starting point.

spans.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation,
conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
Now we are engaged in a great civil war,
testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.

lead.text: Lincoln's opening sentence is more than a date. It says that the nation was “conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal”, and that is a premise, a claim from which an argument can run. The next sentence runs it: “Now we are engaged in a great civil war, testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.” If the nation was founded on that proposition, then a war fought over whether such a nation can survive is a test of the proposition *itself*. That movement from **premise to consequence** is [[logos|Persuasion through reasoning from reasons to a conclusion. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and it carries the whole speech.

The other two appeals are at work as well. Lincoln speaks as the one who dedicates the ground, in the name of the nation (“We have come to dedicate a portion of that field”), and he gives the dead their due with “the last full measure of devotion”, a phrase that asks the audience to feel what they gave. The figure marks them alongside the reasoning, and you may notice how little space the reasoning needs because the other two appeals have prepared the ground.

spans.text: We have come to dedicate a portion of that field,
as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live.
that from these honored dead we take increased devotion to that cause for which they gave
the last full measure of devotion
Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and
dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.

lead.text: Aristotle's three appeals describe how a speech persuades, but they leave out when and where it is given. Greek writers on rhetoric had a word for that as well, **kairos**, meaning the right or opportune moment, and it is often added to the three as a fourth appeal. A speech has kairos when it uses its occasion: a speaker at the opening of a library who says “We are standing where the old school burned down” is doing so, because the place *itself* supplies part of the argument, and so is a coach who says “We are three goals down at half time, and that is exactly when this team has always found its best football”, because the moment is what makes the words land.

A useful test is to ask whether the speech could be moved to another day or another place without losing anything. If it could, it has little kairos, and if it works only here and now, it has a great deal.

model.source: An invented speech at a library opening

spans.text: We are standing where the old school burned down.
Tonight it is a reading room, and that says what this town values.
We are three goals down at half time, and that is exactly when this team has always found its best football.

reveal.text: Douglass's answer to his own question is that the day reveals “the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim”, so the occasion becomes his evidence. Lincoln does the same with the ground beneath him: “We are met on a great battle-field of that war.”

spans.text: What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?
I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.
We are met on a great battle-field of that war.

blocks.text: On 5 July 1852 Frederick Douglass stood up in Rochester, New York, before an audience gathered to mark American independence, and began by saying that he was *not* included in the celebration. He had to persuade people who admired the Declaration of Independence that they were failing its principles, and he had one speech in which to do it. What can a speaker do, in a single speech, to make an audience trust them, feel something and follow their reasoning?

Aristotle, writing his Rhetoric in the fourth century BC, answered that a speech persuades through the character of the speaker, through the feelings it stirs in the audience and through the reasons it gives, and the moment at which a speech is given matters as much as any of them. With those ideas you can take a persuasive passage apart, whether it is Douglass in Rochester or a charity letter on your doormat, and say which of them a sentence is working through and why it works on the people it was written for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the appeal a sentence makes, date a speech from its opening, and say how a speaker uses the moment.
intro.whyItMatters: Persuasion depends on trust, feeling and reasons together, and naming them lets you see why a speech works instead of only feeling that it does.

recap.keyIdea: A speaker persuades through ethos, pathos and logos, and the best speeches also fit their moment, which the Greeks called kairos.

blocks.text: Aristotle named three appeals: **ethos**, which works through the speaker's character and standing, **pathos**, which works through the audience's feelings, and **logos**, which works through reasoning from reasons to a conclusion. Douglass leans on ethos and pathos to unsettle an audience that has come to celebrate, and Lincoln reasons from the founding premise of 1776 to the test the war has set.
Both speeches also use **kairos**, the right moment, so that the occasion itself becomes part of the argument.

recap.nextHook: Next we look closely at the sentences speakers use to make their appeals work, such as repetition, balance and reversal.

lessons.title: Figures of repetition and balance

lead.text: Winston Churchill, speaking to the House of Commons on 4 June 1940, said: “we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills.” The phrase “we shall fight” returns at the start of each [[clause|A finite verb with its subject. Met in 'Inside a clause'.]], and what changes is only the place. Repetition of this kind, at the start of successive clauses, is called **anaphora**, from a Greek word meaning a carrying back, since each clause carries the listener back to the same beginning.

Why does it work? Because **the frame stays still**, the listener's attention goes to whatever is *changing*, and the changing part is the part the speaker wants noticed. The repetition also builds momentum, and in a speech it gives the audience something to expect and then to feel the weight of. The King James Bible does the same thing in Ecclesiastes: “A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted”.

afterFigure.text: Anaphora is not confined to the beginnings of sentences or to oratory. Wherever the same words open a run of clauses, the writer is using the frame to make the rest stand out.

spans.text: in the fields and in the streets,
pluck up that which is planted

lead.text: Notice what else Dickens does. “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times” has a repeated frame, but the two endings are opposites, and the matching shape makes the opposition easy to see. Putting contrasting ideas in parallel form is called **antithesis**, from a Greek word meaning a setting against. Neil Armstrong's line from the Moon on 20 July 1969 does it too, as it is commonly quoted: “That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”

In both examples the two halves have the same shape, and that shape tells the reader to compare them. **The comparison is the point**, since a small step and a giant leap are meant to be seen together. An antithesis, then, makes a choice or a contrast vivid, and it is a favourite device of anyone who has to say that two things differ.

afterFigure.text: Figures can *share* a passage. Dickens's clauses are anaphora because of the repeated “it was”, and antithesis because of the contrasting endings, and both can be true of the same words.

model.source: Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities, opening

lead.text: At Gettysburg in 1863 Lincoln said: “The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here.” Look at how the two halves are built.

reveal.text: It is antithesis. Lincoln's point is that words matter less than deeds, and the sentence makes the point by setting the two side by side so that the listener can feel which is *heavier*.

workedSteps.text: The halves have the same shape: “what we say here” and “what they did here”, each a clause that does the work of a noun, and each ending on the same word.
Their meanings are opposed: *saying* against *doing*, and “we” against “they”, and the verbs of the larger sentence also run opposite ways, “little note” against “never forget”.
Put those two observations together, and the question is which figure they make.

spans.text: The world will little note, nor long remember

lead.text: Some balanced sentences do more than set two things side by side: they turn the words round. John F. Kennedy said in his inaugural address on 20 January 1961, “ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.” The key terms come in the order *country, you* in the first half and *you, country* in the second. A figure in which the second half repeats the terms of the first in reverse order, A B then B A, is called **chiasmus**, after the Greek letter *chi*, which is shaped like an X, because the terms cross.

The reversal is more than decoration, because **it changes the relation**. In Kennedy's sentence the country is first the giver and then the receiver, and the reversal states the whole argument of the speech in a single turn. A proverb works the same way: “You can take the boy out of the country, but you can't take the country out of the boy”. A strict name for a chiasmus that repeats the very same words is *antimetabole*, which you will see in some books.

Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence (1776) lists the rights that every person has: “Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness”. A series of three parallel members like this is a **tricolon**, from the Greek *kolon*, a limb or clause, and it has a long history because **three feels complete**. Two items can seem a pair and four can seem a list, whereas three gives a sense of rhythm that arrives, lands and finishes.

A tricolon can be as small as a starter's call, “Ready, steady, go”, or as large as three clauses, and what matters is that the members are *alike in form* so that the listener hears them as a set. Often the third member is the longest, as in Jefferson's, and that gives the series a little push at the end.

spans.text: shall not perish from the earth.

lead.text: The four figures are *not* exclusive. In the sentence “we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground”, Lincoln repeats “we can not” at the start of each clause, which is [[anaphora|Repetition of the same words at the start of successive clauses. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and the three verbs dedicate, consecrate and hallow form a tricolon. Churchill's “we shall fight” is a single frame repeated, and Dickens combines anaphora with antithesis.

A good habit when you read is to ask two questions of any passage: **what is repeated, and what changes**. If the repeated part is the opening, you are looking at anaphora; if the ends are opposed, antithesis; if the terms return in reverse order, chiasmus; and if there are three members alike in form, a tricolon. Then ask what the figure does for the argument, since each does something different. Anaphora builds momentum and insistence, antithesis sharpens a choice, chiasmus turns a relation round, and tricolon gives a feeling of completeness.

reveal.text: Caesar's line is a tricolon, because it has three parallel members, and an anaphora, because they open alike. The figures overlap here too, and a short sentence is enough to hold both.

blocks.text: Here are two sentences with almost the same meaning. The first says, “Do not wonder what the nation can offer you; think instead about what you can contribute to it.” The second says, “ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.” The second is what John F. Kennedy said in his inaugural address on 20 January 1961, and it is the one that people quote.

The meaning is no better in the second version, so the difference lies in its *shape*, in the way its two halves are built to answer each other. Shapes like this have had names since the teachers of rhetoric in ancient Greece and Rome, and once you can name one you can say what it does for an argument, why it makes a line stay in the memory, and how to build the same shape into a sentence of your own.

intro.whyItMatters: A figure of speech is a decision about shape, and seeing the shape explains why some sentences stay in the memory and others disappear.

recap.keyIdea: Anaphora repeats an opening, antithesis sets opposed ideas in matching form, chiasmus reverses its terms, and a tricolon makes three parallel members.

blocks.text: **Anaphora** repeats the opening of successive clauses so that attention falls on what changes, and **antithesis** sets opposed ideas in matching form so that the contrast can be seen at once. **Chiasmus** repeats terms in reverse order, A B then B A, and turns a relation round, while a **tricolon** gives three parallel members and a sense of completeness.
The figures overlap, so the way to read a passage is to ask what is repeated and what changes, and then what the shape does for the argument.

recap.nextHook: Next we move from the sentence to the line of verse, and learn to count syllables and place the beats of iambic pentameter.

lessons.title: Metre and scansion

lead.text: Start with the smallest unit of verse. A **syllable** is one pulse of sound, a vowel sound with the consonants that cling to it, and you can count them by tapping once for each: “compare” has two, “summer's” has two, and “day” has one. Some syllables in a line are said more strongly than others, a little louder and longer, as the second syllable of “com-PARE” is, and that extra weight is called **stress**.

Now say a nursery rhyme aloud: HICK-o-ry DICK-o-ry DOCK. The stresses return at regular distances, and **the regularity is what makes the line chant**. The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that a poem repeats from line to line is called its **metre**, and the figure marks the stresses in two nursery rhymes so that you can see the pattern as well as hear it.

afterFigure.text: Metre is a *pattern* and not a *measurement*. Two lines can have the same number of syllables and different metres, so both counts matter, how many syllables there are and where the stresses fall.

lead.text: The commonest pattern in English poetry since the sixteenth century is a weak syllable followed by a strong one, as in “com-PARE”. A pair like that is called an **iamb**, and the unit in which verse is measured, here one weak syllable with its strong neighbour, is called a **foot**. Five iambs make a line of ten syllables with the beats on *every second* syllable, and a line of five feet is a pentameter, so the whole pattern is **iambic pentameter**: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.

Shakespeare wrote his sonnets and most of his plays in it, and so did Milton in his sonnets. In Sonnet 18, “Thou art more lovely and more temperate”, a beat falls on every second syllable, and Romeo's “But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?” does the same (Romeo and Juliet, 2.2). Many critics have noted that the pattern is close to the natural rhythm of English speech, which may be why it lasted.

To read the metre of a line, you mark which syllables carry the beats, and the marking is called **scansion**. The pattern is a frame laid over the words, and the words do not always fit it as speech would have them. In “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?”, the beats fall on *I*, *pare*, *to*, *sum* and *day*, and an ordinary speaker would hardly stress “I” or “to” at all. The frame asks us to give those syllables a little more weight than speech would.

That is the reason scansion is a matter of judgement as well as counting. A stress is only ever stronger than its neighbours, and the same word can be strong in one line and weak in the next. If the first syllable count comes out wrong, the beats will not fall where the pattern needs them, and so **the syllable count always comes first**.

steps.headline: Scan Milton's “They also serve who only stand and wait”

lead.text: The line is the last of Milton's sonnet on his blindness, “When I consider how my light is spent”. The method is to count the syllables, mark the strong ones, and then read the line against the frame.

workedSteps.text: Count the syllables by tapping: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / wait. That makes ten, which is the length of a regular line of [[iambic pentameter|Five iambs to a line: ten syllables with the beats on the even ones. Met earlier in this lesson.]].

Now mark the strong syllables, which are the ones that carry the sense: *al* in “also”, *serve*, *on* in “only”, *stand* and *wait*. If the line is regular, each of them sits in an even-numbered place, where an iamb puts its beat.
Last, check one of them against the frame: number the syllables from the first and find where the beat on “stand” falls.

steps.headline: Place the beats in “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”

lead.text: This is Sonnet 18, line 3. The line is regular, so the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables.

reveal.text: It falls on syllable 6, the first syllable of “darling”, which is the strong syllable of that word. The remaining beats follow on 8 (“buds”) and 10 (“May”).

workedSteps.text: Count the syllables: rough / winds / do / shake / the / dar / ling / buds / of / May. That makes ten.
The first beat falls on syllable 2, “winds”, and the second on syllable 4, “shake”, because each iamb puts its strong syllable second.
The remaining beats follow the same rule, and the question is on which syllable the third one falls.

lead.text: Not every line has exactly ten syllables. Macbeth says, in the fifth act, “To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow”, and when you tap it out you get to-MOR-row and to-MOR-row and to-MOR-row, which comes to eleven. The last syllable, “-row”, is weak, and it comes after the final beat. A weak syllable that follows the last beat in this way is called a **feminine ending**, in the traditional name for it, and a line that ends on its final beat has a masculine ending.

Notice what the extra syllable does. The line stops stressing and then trails off, and a speaker like Macbeth, who is running out of reasons to go on, is well served by a line that trails off. The regular pentameter is *still there* underneath, since the first ten syllables are an ordinary pattern of iambs, and the eleventh is simply added.

reveal.text: The extra syllable comes from the last word, “shaken”. The line is a regular pentameter with one weak syllable added after the final beat, which is exactly what a feminine ending is.

lead.text: Not all verse rises. “Twinkle, twinkle, little star” starts each foot on the strong syllable, TWIN-kle, with the weak one after it, and a foot with a strong syllable followed by a weak one is a **trochee**. It is the iamb *turned round*, a falling foot where the iamb rises, and it gives lines a driving, chanting sound.

The number of feet gives the line its length, and each length has a name from the Greek for the number: three feet make a **trimeter**, four a **tetrameter** and five a pentameter. A name for a metre therefore has two parts, the kind of foot and the number, so that a line of four iambs is iambic tetrameter and a line of four trochees is trochaic tetrameter. The figure compares the falling rhythm of the nursery rhyme with the rising rhythm of Sonnet 18.

afterFigure.text: So the vocabulary of metre is small. **Say which foot it is, say how many there are**, and you have described the metre of a line in two words.

reveal.text: Four trochees make a trochaic tetrameter, and the figure sets the witches beside “Twinkle, twinkle”. Shakespeare gives his spell-casters a chant that sounds nothing like the rising rhythm in which his noblemen speak.

blocks.text: Say these two lines aloud. The first is Shakespeare's: “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?” The second asks the same thing in different words: “Should I compare you with a day in summer?” Both are perfectly good English, yet the first has a beat that you can tap on a table, and the second does *not* settle into one.

The beat comes from the order of strong and weak syllables. In Shakespeare's line the stresses fall on every second syllable, while in the paraphrase they come at uneven intervals, so no pattern has time to settle. Counting the syllables of a line and marking the strong ones is called scansion, and with it you can hear the pattern under a line you have never seen, say what that pattern is called, and notice the places where a poet breaks it on purpose.

recap.keyIdea: Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, and a line is named by its foot and the number of feet.

blocks.text: A line of verse has a **metre**, a pattern of weak and strong syllables, and the usual English unit is the **iamb**, a weak syllable followed by a strong one. Five iambs make iambic pentameter, a line of ten syllables with the beats on the even ones, and the same units make tetrameter with four feet or trimeter with three.

A **feminine ending** adds a weak syllable after the last beat, and a **trochee** reverses the iamb so that the foot falls from strong to weak. Scansion begins with the syllable count and then lays the pattern over the words.

lessons.title: Sound and image

lead.text: Say “Betty Botter bought some butter, but she said the butter's bitter” and your lips will tell you what the line is doing: it repeats the same opening sound, b, in word after word. Repeating a consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words is called **alliteration**. The word means the *sound*, not the *letter*, so that “knight” and “night” alliterate with each other, while “cat” and “city” do not.

What does it do for a line? It binds the words that share the sound, so that they seem to belong together, and it gives the line a texture that the ear notices before the mind does. Keats begins “To Autumn” with “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness”, where the soft m sounds fall on the two words that matter most to the picture. Critics are cautious about saying that a particular sound *means* a particular thing, but nobody doubts that **repeated sounds draw attention to the words that carry them**.

Poets can also repeat a vowel sound. Edgar Allan Poe's “The Bells” has the phrase “Hear the mellow wedding bells”, in which “mellow”, “wedding” and “bells” share the same short e sound, though their consonants differ. Repeating a vowel sound in nearby words is called **assonance**, and unlike [[alliteration|Repeating a consonant sound at the start of nearby words. Met earlier in this lesson.]] it does not depend on where in the word the sound falls.

Because the sound can fall in the middle of a word, assonance is quieter than alliteration and harder to catch. Look at Sonnet 30, line 4: “And with old woes new wail my dear time's waste”. The long o of “old” and “woes” echoes inside the line, and the long a of “wail” and “waste” echoes a few words later, so the line sounds closed in on itself, as grief does.

afterFigure.text: Assonance is a matter of *ear* and not of *spelling*, which is why you have to say a line aloud to find it. Words that look alike on the page, such as “still” and “bride”, may share no vowel sound, and words that look different may share one.

lead.text: So far we have listened to lines, and now we look at the pictures they make. “The classroom was like a zoo” compares a classroom with a zoo, and the word *like* tells us so. A comparison announced by “like” or “as” is a **simile**. Take the signal away and say “The classroom was a zoo”, and you have a **metaphor**, which does not compare two things but declares that one *is* the other.

A metaphor is not a lie. It asks the reader to carry the qualities of one thing over to the other, noise and chaos from the zoo to the classroom, and to leave behind what does not apply, such as the bars. Shakespeare gives us the best-known example in As You Like It, 2.7: “All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players”.

afterFigure.text: The test is mechanical: **look for the signalling word**. If “like” or “as” stands between the two things, it is a simile, and if the two things are joined by plain “is” or by no word at all, it is a metaphor. The effect differs too, because a simile keeps the two things apart and a metaphor joins them.

lead.text: Every figure of this kind has two parts. The critic I. A. Richards, in *The Philosophy of Rhetoric* (1936), named them: the **tenor** is the thing being described, and the **vehicle** is the image used to describe it. In “Juliet is the sun”, Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle, and in Burns's “O my Luve's like a red, red rose”, the beloved is the tenor and the rose the vehicle. The two parts work for simile and metaphor alike.

Sometimes the vehicle is never named. In “The committee chair growled and snapped at every question”, the chair is the tenor, and “growled and snapped” belongs to an animal, a dog, although the sentence does not say so. The reader **supplies the vehicle** from the verbs, and the pleasure of the figure is partly in that act of supplying.

Part of that effect comes from Keats's choice of sounds, the m that opens “mists” and “mellow” and the slow vowels between them, and part from his choice of pictures, since in the very next line autumn becomes a person, the “Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun”. Sound and image are the two ways a line works on you before you have thought about it, and once you can name the devices behind each you can say exactly where a line's effect comes from instead of only feeling it.

A **simile** announces a comparison with “like” or “as”, and a **metaphor** declares that one thing is another.
In either figure the **tenor** is the thing described and the **vehicle** is the image that describes it, and the vehicle is sometimes left for the reader to find.

lessons.title: The sonnet and its turn

lead.text: Two words rhyme when their endings sound alike from the last stressed vowel onwards, and it is the *sound* that counts and not the *spelling*: “night” and “write” rhyme, though they look unlike. To describe how a poem rhymes, we give each ending sound a letter, starting with A for the first, and each time a new sound appears we use the next letter. Here is Jane Taylor's “Twinkle, twinkle, little star” (1806): *star*, *are*, *high*, *sky* gives A A B B, because the first two lines share a sound and so do the last two. The string of letters is the poem's **rhyme scheme**.

Lines are often grouped into small units, and a group of four lines is a **quatrain**, from the Latin for four. Sonnet 18 opens with a quatrain that ends *day, temperate, May, date*, and its scheme is therefore A B A B, since the first and third lines share a sound and so do the second and fourth.

A sonnet has fourteen lines, and in the form that Shakespeare used, which was printed in his *Sonnets* of 1609, they fall into three quatrains and two lines more. Each quatrain has its own pair of rhymes, in the pattern A B A B, then C D C D, then E F E F, and the last two lines rhyme with each other, G G. A pair of rhyming lines that closes a poem like this is a **couplet**, and the full scheme is ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

Read the figure's two sonnets and you can see the shape: the sounds change at every quatrain, so that each one feels like a *separate* step, and then the rhyme settles into a pair that sounds like a conclusion. The shape suits **an argument that moves in stages** and ends with a summing-up.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the rhyme scheme does not decide what the quatrains say. It sets up a rhythm of expectation, and the poet works with it or against it, which is what we turn to next.

Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st,
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st,
So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:
O no! it is an ever-fixed mark
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wandering bark,
Whose worth’s unknown, although his height be taken.

Within his bending sickle’s compass come;

lead.text: Fourteen lines are enough room for one thought and a change of direction, and a good deal of the pleasure of a sonnet is in the change. The place where the argument turns is called the **volta**, the Italian word for a turn. It is often marked by a word like *but*, *yet* or *and yet*, which tells the reader that what follows will not go the way the poem has been going.

Sonnet 18 shows it plainly. For eight lines Shakespeare asks whether the beloved can be compared with a summer's day and finds that summer will not do: it is rough, too hot, too brief, and “every fair from fair sometime declines”. Then line 9 opens with “But thy eternal summer shall not fade”, and the argument swings round to say that the beloved, unlike summer, will last. The volta is **the hinge on which the whole poem swings**.

The sonnet began in Italy in the thirteenth century, and its name comes from the Italian *sonetto*, a little song. Petrarch, in the fourteenth century, made it famous, and so the Italian form is called the Petrarchan sonnet. English poets took it up in the sixteenth century. It divides the fourteen lines unequally, into an eight-line **octave** rhyming ABBAABBA, which states a problem or a feeling, and a six-line **sestet** with a pattern such as CDECDE, which answers it.

The two parts are of unequal length, and the turn falls between them, at the ninth line, so that **the shape of the poem carries the shape of the argument**. The Shakespearean form can turn there too, as Sonnet 18 does, but the Italian form builds the turn into its structure.

lead.text: Milton wrote a sonnet in the Italian form after he had lost his sight, and it begins “When I consider how my light is spent”. The figure sets out its opening [[octave|The first eight lines of an Italian sonnet. Met earlier in this lesson.]] with the word that ends each line.

reveal.text: Only two, A and B, each used four times, and that is why the octave sounds so *tightly knit*. Milton's complaint is held in a tight rhyming frame, and the sestet that follows gets new sounds to answer it.

workedSteps.text: The first line ends on “spent”, which gives the first sound, A, and the second ends on “wide”, which gives the second, B.
The other six lines end on “hide”, “bent”, “present”, “chide”, “denied” and “prevent”, and each of them either repeats one of those two sounds or brings in a new one.
Give each line its letter, and the question is how many different rhyme sounds the octave uses.
