lines.text: When I consider how my light is spent,
Ere half my days, in this dark world and wide,
And that one Talent which is death to hide,
Lodged with me useless, though my Soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, lest he returning chide;
“Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?”
I fondly ask. But Patience, to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, “God doth not need
Either man's work or his own gifts. Who best
Bear his mild yoke, they serve him best. His state
Is kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed
And post o'er land and ocean without rest;
They also serve who only stand and wait.”
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:
O no! it is an ever-fixed mark
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wandering bark,
Whose worth’s unknown, although his height be taken.
Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks
Within his bending sickle’s compass come;
Love alters not with his brief hours and weeks,
But bears it out even to the edge of doom.
If this be error and upon me proved,
I never writ, nor no man ever loved.
When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes
I all alone beweep my outcast state,
And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries,
And look upon myself, and curse my fate,
Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
Featur’d like him, like him with friends possess’d,
Desiring this man’s art, and that man’s scope,
With what I most enjoy contented least;
Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising,
Haply I think on thee, and then my state,
Like to the lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;
For thy sweet love remember’d such wealth brings
That then I scorn to change my state with kings.
Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,

So long as men can breathe, or eyes can see,

lead.text: The [[volta|The turn in a sonnet's argument. Met earlier in this lesson.]] does not have to come at line 9. In Sonnet 30, Shakespeare spends twelve lines in mourning, calling up “remembrance of things past”, weeping for friends long dead and paying again for griefs he thought were settled. If we read on, the argument seems to be that old losses can never be made good. Then the couplet begins with “But if the while I think on thee, dear friend”, and it says that the thought of the beloved restores every loss and ends every sorrow.

Here the turn is saved for the end, and it is stronger for being *late*. The same is true of Milton's sonnet, where the turn comes in the middle of line 8, as the octave closes and the sestet begins. The lesson is to **look for the word that reverses the direction**, and not to count on its being at a fixed line.

afterFigure.text: So the rule of thumb is that the turn marks a change of direction, and the form tells you where to look first. In an Italian sonnet it is usually at the ninth line, in Shakespeare's it may be there or in the couplet, and a few poets place it elsewhere.

lines.text: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red, than her lips red:
If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,
But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
And in some perfumes is there more delight
Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
That music hath a far more pleasing sound:
I grant I never saw a goddess go;
My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare,
As any she belied with false compare.

A **sonnet** is a poem of fourteen lines, and English poets have kept coming back to the form for nearly five hundred years because fourteen lines give a thought room to be stated, challenged and settled. recap.nextHook: Next we turn to prose and ask who is telling a story, and how an author can let us hear a character's thoughts inside the narrator's voice.

lessons.title: Who sees and who speaks

lead.text: Every story is told by someone, and that someone is the **narrator**. The narrator is not the author. It is a voice that the author has chosen, and the first thing that voice tells you, often without saying so, is how it stands to the events. A narrator who is also a character in the story and says “I” writes in the **first person**. Edgar Allan Poe's “The Tell-Tale Heart” begins, “True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?”, and the narrator is both telling the tale and living in it.

A narrator who stays outside the story and refers to the characters as *he*, *she* and *they* writes in the **third person**. Jane Austen opens *Persuasion* in that way: “Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never took up any book but the Baronetage”. The test for the person of a narrator is simply **whether the narrator says “I”** about their own part in the story.

Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own amusement, never took up any book but the Baronetage;
Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence;
True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

lead.text: A third-person narrator is not bound to see what a character sees. Take the sentence “Everyone in Little Wick knew that the new vicar would not last the winter, though he himself was sure he would.” The narrator knows what the whole village thinks, and also knows what the vicar thinks, and sets the two side by side, which no single person in the village could do. A narrator who knows the thoughts of all the characters, and the whole of the story, is called **omniscient**, from the Latin for all-knowing.

That wide knowledge lets an omniscient narrator do something a character cannot, which is to *comment*. The narrator can tell us what is true as against what the characters suppose, and can let us see the gap between them. The figure shows two examples in which the narrator knows something about the village that the village does not know about itself.

lead.text: There are three ways to report what a character thinks. In **direct speech** the thought appears in quotation marks, in the character's own words: “This cake is a disaster!” In indirect speech the narrator reports it with a verb of thinking: Ben thought that the cake was a disaster. Between them stands a third way, in which the narrator simply writes, “The cake was a disaster!”, and the sentence has no quotation marks, no “Ben thought”, and the grammar of the narrator, in the [[third person|A narrator outside the story who refers to the characters as he, she and they. Met earlier in this lesson.]] and past tense, but the exclamation is plainly *Ben's*.

That third way is **free indirect discourse**, and it is free in the sense that it has dropped the reporting verb. It lets the reader hear a character from inside while the narrator keeps telling the story, and Jane Austen was one of the first novelists to use it often and well. The figure shows how the direct thought, the indirect report and the free indirect sentence line up for two characters.

What stays the same is **the character's attitude**, the exclamation and the idiom.

lead.text: Take a story in which Anna comes home after a bad day, and see how her thought can be written in three ways.

workedSteps.text: In direct speech her thought would be “What a dreadful day it has been!”, in quotation marks, with the verb in her own present tense.
In indirect speech the narrator would report it with a reporting verb: Anna thought that it had been a dreadful day. The exclamation is *gone* and so are the quotation marks.

In [[free indirect discourse|A character's own words or thoughts in the narrator's third person and past tense, with no reporting verb. Met earlier in this lesson.]] the narrator writes “What a dreadful day it had been!” and leaves out the “Anna thought”. The question is what that sentence keeps from Anna's own thought.

reveal.text: Compare “It was a wretched business indeed!” with “She thought that it was a wretched business”. The reporting clause has been dropped, and with it the distance between Emma and the narrator.

It was a wretched business indeed!
Ben thought that the cake was a disaster.

lead.text: Novels move between these modes without *announcing* it. In one paragraph a narrator may report what a character does, quote what she says, and drop into what she thinks, and a reader who knows the three marks can tell which is which. Plain **narration** reports actions from outside: “Mia hung up her coat.” Direct speech is in quotation marks: “Where have you been?” asked her father. A sentence in the character's idiom with the narrator's person and tense is free indirect: “Honestly, what a day it had been!”

The sorting rule has **three questions**. Are there quotation marks, and if so it is direct speech. Does the sentence report an action in the narrator's own voice, and if so it is narration. Does it carry a character's exclamation or opinion in the third person and past tense, with nothing to say who is thinking, and if so it is free indirect discourse.

spans.text: “Where have you been?” asked her father.
Honestly, what a day it had been!

reveal.text: The figure's second view gives two more: Emma's “Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!” is free indirect, and so is “but it was all confusion”, while “She looked back as well as she could” is plain narration. Austen moves between them in a single sentence.

spans.text: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
(2) The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
(3) How she could have been so deceived!
Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!
She looked back as well as she could;

lessons.orientation: Distinguish first- from third-person narration and hear an omniscient narrator's irony. Recognise free indirect discourse in Austen.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence from chapter 16 of Jane Austen's Emma (1815), after Mr Elton's unwelcome proposal: “Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!” It is in the third person and the past tense, like the narration around it, yet the dismay is plainly *Emma's*, since the narrator has no reason to be upset by a proposal. There are no quotation marks and no “she thought”, and still we hear her.

Every story is told by someone, and the teller can stand outside the characters, speak as one of them, or let a character's own voice slip into the narration as Austen does here. Asking who is telling a story, and whose feelings colour a given sentence, tells you what you are being shown, whose view it is and how far to trust it, which is why it is the first question to put to any passage of prose.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say who is telling a story and from where, hear an omniscient narrator's irony, and recognise a character's thought inside the narration.
intro.whyItMatters: Who tells a story decides what you know and how far you can trust it, and noticing the voice is the first step in reading prose closely.

recap.keyIdea: A narrator's person and knowledge shape a story, and free indirect discourse lets a character's voice speak inside the narrator's third person.

blocks.text: A **narrator** writes in the **first person** when it is also a character and says “I”, and in the **third person** when it stays outside. A third-person narrator who knows everything is **omniscient**, and can comment on what the characters do not know.

**Free indirect discourse** lets a character's own exclamation or idiom enter the narration in the third person and past tense with no reporting verb, so that you hear the character without quotation marks.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask when a narrator's voice, or a character's, says one thing and means another, and learn to tell three kinds of irony apart.

lessons.title: Irony and unreliable narrators

lead.text: Suppose a customer has just had a bowl of soup land in his lap and says, “Lovely, thank you.” His words say that the soup was lovely, and everyone in the room knows that he means nothing of the kind. That gap between what is said and what is meant is the heart of **irony**, and when it lies in a speaker's own words the figure is **verbal irony**: the speaker says one thing and means something close to its opposite, relying on the *listener* to see it.

How does the listener see it? From the context, since **the soup in his lap is what shows that the words cannot be meant straight**, and often from tone as well. On the page there is no tone, so a writer has to put the context in the scene, as the figure does for two invented speakers. In each case the line is true as a sentence and false as a meaning, and the distance between the two is where the irony lives.

model.speaker: The customer
model.said: The soup was lovely and he is grateful.
model.known: Soup has just landed in his lap, and everyone in the room can see it.

model.speaker: A commuter
model.line: I do love standing in a queue.
model.known: She has stood in the rain for forty minutes, and so has everyone around her.

reveal.text: Four repetitions, and the phrase is the same each time. What changes is what the crowd has just heard, so that the same words are heard first as respect and last as an accusation.

spans.text: So are they all, all honourable men,
But Brutus says he was ambitious,
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;
Yet Brutus says he was ambitious;

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, and so his charge that Caesar was ambitious must be true.
model.known: Brutus helped kill Caesar, and each repetition invites the crowd to doubt the word.

lead.text: [[Irony|The gap between what seems to be so and what is. Met earlier in this lesson.]] can also be built up over a whole speech. In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar (3.2), Mark Antony has been allowed to speak at Caesar's funeral on condition that he says nothing against the conspirators, so he praises them: “For Brutus is an honourable man”. But he follows the praise with facts that Brutus's charge of ambition cannot account for, that Caesar brought captives home whose ransoms filled the public treasury and that he three times refused a crown that Antony offered him. Each time, the refrain “Brutus is an honourable man” comes back, and **each time it means a little less**.

By the end the phrase has turned over, and the words that meant praise at the start now mean the reverse. The crowd that began by trusting Brutus finishes the scene calling for revenge on his friends. Antony never says a word *against* Brutus; he lets repetition and the facts do it for him.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: For Brutus is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, so his charge against Caesar must be true.
model.known: The crowd still trusts Brutus, so the line sounds like respect.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And, sure, he is an honourable man.
model.said: Brutus is honourable, so his charge against Caesar must be true.
model.known: The crowd has heard about the ransoms and the refused crown, and now hears the opposite.

lead.text: A different kind of irony does not depend on what anyone says, but on what the audience knows. When a character speaks in ignorance of something the audience has been shown, the character's words carry **a meaning he cannot hear**. This is **dramatic irony**, so called because it flourishes in plays, though it works in films and novels too. Take a retelling in which Little Red Riding Hood says, “What big teeth you have!” The line is an innocent remark about her grandmother, and for us who have watched the wolf swallow the grandmother, it is a line of terror.

The figure's second case runs on the same plan: a detective says, “I would trust Hobbs with my life”, while we have just seen Hobbs slip the silver into his coat. Notice that the speaker means what he says. It is the *audience's* extra knowledge that opens a gap, and the speaker does not know that it exists.

model.speaker: Little Red Riding Hood
model.said: A polite remark about her grandmother’s teeth.
model.known: The figure in the bed is the wolf, and the audience has seen it swallow the grandmother.

model.speaker: The detective
model.line: I would trust Hobbs with my life.
model.known: The audience saw Hobbs slip the silver into his coat.

reveal.text: Romeo says that death has had no power yet upon her beauty, and he thinks he is describing a corpse. The audience knows he is looking at a sleeper, and the figure's second view shows another example: Duncan praises the pleasant seat of the castle where he will be murdered that night.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: Death, that hath suck’d the honey of thy breath, / Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty:
model.said: Juliet is dead, and her beauty is death's strange mercy.
model.known: Juliet has taken the Friar's sleeping potion and is about to wake.

model.speaker: Duncan
model.line: This castle hath a pleasant seat.
model.said: The castle is a welcoming place to rest.
model.known: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth have resolved to murder Duncan there that night.

lead.text: The third kind needs neither a speaker who means the opposite nor an audience that knows more. In **situational irony** events themselves turn against the purpose that set them going. In O. Henry's story “The Gift of the Magi” (1905), a young wife sells her hair to buy a chain for her husband's watch, while he sells the watch to buy her a set of combs for her hair. Each gift is a treat for the one who loves, and each has made the other gift useless.

The same shape appears in a safety inspector who trips over a loose rug during her own inspection. What makes these ironic is **the reversal**, since the outcome is the opposite of what was intended or expected, and we notice the reversal because we know the intention. Nobody has to say anything, and nobody has to know anything beforehand, since the irony is in *how things turn out*.

model.source: O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi
model.speaker: Della and Jim
model.line: Combs for her hair, bought with his watch, and a chain for his watch, bought with her hair.
model.said: Each gift is a treat for the one they love.
model.known: Each has sold the thing the other’s gift was meant for, so neither gift can be used.

model.speaker: A safety inspector
model.line: She trips over a loose rug during her own inspection.
model.said: She is there to find hazards and keep people safe.
model.known: She is the one who falls over a hazard she failed to see.

model.speaker: Romeo
model.line: I thought all for the best.
model.said: Stepping between the fighters will stop the duel.
model.known: Tybalt's thrust under Romeo's arm kills Mercutio: the peace-making makes the death possible.

model.speaker: Mark Antony
model.line: And, sure, he is an honourable man.
model.known: Antony means the opposite, and the crowd hears it.

lead.text: The last kind of irony is in the telling of a story. A [[narrator|The voice that tells the story. Met in 'Who sees and who speaks'.]] is **unreliable**, a term the critic Wayne Booth introduced in *The Rhetoric of Fiction* (1961), when readers have reason to doubt that the account is true or complete. The evidence is usually in the telling itself. A narrator who announces, “I have never been calmer in my life”, and then counts the spoons three times and checks the lock again is showing us the opposite of calm, and the gap between claim and behaviour is the irony.

Another narrator says, “I never touched it,” and adds that the icing was already on his chin when he found the cake, and the second statement contradicts the first. In both cases the narrator is the only source we have, and yet we can see what he does not say. So reading an unreliable narrator means **trusting your own eyes over his words**, while still enjoying the voice.

spans.text: I have never been calmer in my life.
I counted the spoons three times to be sure, and I locked the door, and then I checked the lock again.
“and the icing was already on my chin when I found it.”

reveal.text: He says that he heard all things in heaven and earth, and asks “How, then, am I mad?”, and the question proves nothing. He says that he loved the old man, who had never wronged him, yet he describes killing him. The protests are the evidence against him.

spans.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am;
but why will you say that I am mad?
I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell.
Object there was none. Passion there was none.

blocks.text: When Mark Antony tells the Roman crowd that “Brutus is an honourable man”, he is speaking at Caesar's funeral, and he has promised Brutus he will say *nothing* against the men who killed Caesar. By the end of the scene the crowd is calling for those men's blood. Antony has not said a word against Brutus.

What Antony has found is a gap between what a speaker says and what the audience takes him to mean, and a gap of that kind is called **irony**. It can open in more than one place: in a speaker's words, as here, in what an audience knows that a character does not, or in the way events turn out against what someone intended. Telling the kinds apart lets you read what a writer has put under the words, and it shows you when a narrator's own account gives away more than he means it to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell verbal, dramatic and situational irony apart, and spot a narrator whose own account gives them away.
intro.whyItMatters: Irony is how literature says what it cannot say directly, and missing it means reading the opposite of what is meant.

recap.keyIdea: Irony is a gap between what seems to be so and what is: verbal in a speaker's words, dramatic in what an audience knows, and situational in how events turn out.

blocks.text: **Verbal irony** means the opposite of what the words say, **dramatic irony** arises when the audience knows what a character does not, and **situational irony** is an outcome that turns against the purpose that produced it. To tell them apart, ask whether the gap lies in what is said, in what is known or in what happens.
An **unreliable narrator** gives himself away through the telling itself, so that the reader learns to trust what the narrator does and not what he says.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at the shape of a whole story, and ask where its climax falls and how many of its scenes turn between hope and loss.

lessons.title: Structure: arcs and turning scenes

lead.text: Most stories feel as if they climb a hill. At the beginning the trouble is small and the stakes are low, then the stakes mount from scene to scene until a point where everything could go *either way*, and after that point the tension falls as the consequences work themselves out. The figure draws two fairy tales as six scenes each, with the height of each marker showing how high the tension runs, and you can see the hill in both.

Two words help us talk about the shape. The **protagonist** is the character whose fortunes we follow, Cinderella in one story and Red Riding Hood in the other, from the Greek for the first actor. The **climax** is the high point of the hill, the scene where the tension is greatest and the protagonist's fortunes turn sharply. In Cinderella that is midnight, when the spell breaks, and in Red Riding Hood it is the scene in the bed.

afterFigure.text: The heights in the figure are a *reading* and not a *measurement*. Another reader might place a scene one step higher or lower, but most would agree about the shape, with a rise, a peak and a fall, and the shape is what we are learning to see.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

lead.text: In 1863 the German novelist and critic Gustav Freytag published *Die Technik des Dramas*, in which he drew the shape of a play as a pyramid. He named five parts. The **exposition** introduces the place, the time and the people before the conflict begins, and the **rising action** builds the conflict scene by scene. The climax stands at the top, and the **falling action** carries the story down from it. The last part, in a tragedy, is the **catastrophe**, from a Greek word meaning an overturning, in which the hero falls.

The five parts together are called **Freytag's pyramid**, and it is **a useful map even for stories that are not tragedies**. In a fairy tale or a comedy the last part resolves happily, and it is more often called the resolution or the denouement, the French word for an untying. The figure sets the two fairy tales on the pyramid and gives each scene the name of its part.

model.title: Red Riding Hood, named by part

scenes.label: Rising: the wolf in the wood

steps.headline: Romeo and Juliet in five acts

lead.text: Freytag worked from plays divided into **five acts**, and Shakespeare's tragedies divide that way in the standard editions, so Romeo and Juliet gives a good test. Its first act sets out the feud between the Montagues and the Capulets and ends with the feast at which the lovers meet. In the second act they meet again in the garden and are married, and their fortunes are *still on the way up*.

The third act opens with a fight in which Mercutio is killed, and Romeo, in his anger, kills Tybalt and is banished from Verona. In the fourth act the Friar devises a plan to reunite the lovers, and Juliet takes the potion. In the fifth, Romeo hears the news that she is dead before he hears of the plan, and the play ends in the tomb. Where on the pyramid does the high point fall? That is for *you* to say.

reveal.text: The climax is in Act 3. Up to the death of Tybalt, the lovers have been moving towards happiness, and from the banishment onwards everything that happens takes them further from it. The figure's second view shows Cinderella by part, with her high point at midnight, so that you can compare the shapes.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lead.text: The pyramid shows how the tension rises and falls, and a second tool shows how the protagonist's fortunes change. Give each scene a charge at its opening and at its close, + when things stand well for the protagonist and − when they stand badly. A scene in which the sign changes between its opening and its close is a **turning scene**, because something in it has *reversed* the protagonist's position. A scene whose sign stays the same **has held its value** and has changed nothing, however much happens in it.

Cinderella shows the pattern. She begins in the cinders on a −, and the fairy godmother's scene opens on − and closes on +, which turns it. The ball opens on + and closes on +, so it holds its value, and midnight opens on + and closes on −, so it turns again. The figure marks each scene's opening and closing charge, and a story with many turns is one in which fortunes keep reversing.

model.title: Little Red Riding Hood in six scenes

reveal.text: The five turning scenes are the feast, Tybalt's death, the parting after the wedding night, the Friar's plan and the news in Mantua, and between them they take the lovers up and then down. The three scenes that hold their value are the balcony, the wedding and the tomb.

lead.text: Put the two tools together and a pattern appears. In Romeo and Juliet the [[turning scenes|Scenes whose closing value differs from their opening value. Met earlier in this lesson.]] are *not* spread evenly: the lovers' fortunes reverse in quick succession around Act 3, with Tybalt's death and the parting, and the tension is at its highest there. The same is true of Cinderella, whose sharpest reversal is at midnight. The scenes around the climax are the ones in which **fortunes change most quickly**.

That gives you a way to read a plot. Find the peak of the pyramid, which is the climax, and then look at the charges of the scenes near it, since a cluster of turning scenes there is typical. When you meet a story whose peak is quiet, with no turns around it, you have found one that works differently, and that is worth asking about.

reveal.text: The alarm is the tallest marker, and the chase and the split fall away after it. The figure's second view marks the same peak on Romeo and Juliet by act, at Act 3.

model.title: Romeo and Juliet by act, after Freytag

scenes.label: Act 3: Tybalt dies; the wedding night

lessons.orientation: Map a play onto Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes that turn a value from hope to loss or back.

blocks.text: Macbeth opens with its hero coming home from battle as a loyal and praised general. Within a few scenes he has murdered King Duncan and taken the crown, and from the middle of the play his fortunes run downhill, through more killings and a gathering army of enemies, until he is killed in battle at the end. Told that way, the play is a line that climbs and then falls, and most stories you know can be drawn as a line of the same kind, with the tension or the hero's fortunes rising and falling from scene to scene.

In 1863 the German critic Gustav Freytag drew that line for the five-act play as a pyramid, climbing through the first acts to a high point and falling away to the end, and critics have used his shape for novels and films ever since. With it you can place each scene of a story, find the point where the action turns, and count the scenes in which a character's fortunes reverse, which tells you why each scene is there and what it does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place the parts of a story on Freytag's pyramid, find its climax, and count the scenes where the protagonist's fortunes turn.
intro.whyItMatters: Seeing the shape of a story shows you why a scene is there and what it does, which is the foundation of both reading and writing narrative.

recap.keyIdea: A story rises to a climax and falls to its end, and its scenes can be read for whether they turn the protagonist's fortunes.

blocks.text: Freytag's pyramid divides a drama into **exposition**, **rising action**, **climax**, **falling action** and **catastrophe**, and in Romeo and Juliet the climax falls in Act 3, when Tybalt's death turns the lovers' luck against them. The shape works as a map for fairy tales and films too, with a happier last part that is usually called the resolution.
Scoring each scene as + or − at its opening and its close lets you count the **turning scenes**, those in which the protagonist's fortunes reverse, and they tend to gather around the climax.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 18 says “And every fair from fair sometime declines.” Which single word is the finite verb?
hints: Which test from the last screen can you use? Put the line into the past.
Say the line with “once” in front and listen for the word that has to change.
A verb in the past often ends in -ed. Which word could take that ending?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: declines

questions.onCorrect: Told about the past the line would read “declined”, and no other word would move, so “declines” is the finite verb whatever its position.

misconceptions.feedback: “Every” says which fair things are meant, and it would read the same if the line were about the past, so it cannot carry the time.
“Fair” is a noun here, meaning a fair thing, and it is what the line is about; it would stay as it is in the past.
“Sometime” says when, so it is a modifier. Put the line into the past and it stays the same, while the word that says what happens takes -ed.

questions.prompt: The object of “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May” is the phrase “the darling buds of May”. Which single word is its head noun?
hints: Strip away the describing words. Which noun is left as the thing being shaken?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The object is 'the darling buds of May'; its head noun is 'buds'. 'Darling' and 'of May' modify it.

questions.onCorrect: Take away “darling” and “of May” and “shake the buds” still says what the winds do. The other words only describe the noun at the centre.

misconceptions.feedback: “Darling” describes the thing shaken. Look for the noun that it describes.
“May” sits inside “of May”, which tells us which buds. It does not name the thing that is shaken.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 has “If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun.” Which word makes the first clause dependent?
hints: Which word turns a statement into a condition?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'If' subordinates 'snow be white', so that clause cannot stand alone; 'her breasts are dun' can.

questions.onCorrect: “If” turns “snow be white” into a condition, which then waits for “her breasts are dun” to answer it. Without “if” the first clause could stand alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Those words belong to the clause's own content. Look for the small word in front of them that makes the clause wait for a second one.

questions.prompt: Count the finite verbs in Sonnet 116: “Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds”.
hints: A finite verb carries tense: test each word by putting the lines into the past.
Check the main clause, then the clause opened by 'which', then the clause opened by 'when'.
List one verb from each clause and count the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'is', 'alters' and 'finds'. Each anchors a clause.

questions.onCorrect: The three are “is”, “alters” and “finds”, one for each clause. Shakespeare puts the object “alteration” before “finds”, but the verb is still there.

misconceptions.feedback: Two clauses are easy to see, but the one opened by “when” has a verb of its own, with “it” as its subject.
That counts only the first clause. The clauses opened by “which” and “when” each have a finite verb as well.
Check that each word you counted would change with the time. “Alteration” is a noun and stays as it is.

questions.prompt: Frederick Douglass, 1852: “You may rejoice, I must mourn.” How many independent clauses does this sentence hold?
hints: Find each subject and finite verb pair.
Ask whether each clause could stand as a sentence on its own.
Neither clause opens with a subordinator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'You may rejoice' and 'I must mourn'. Each could stand alone, and the comma between them is a deliberate splice.

questions.onCorrect: There are two, “You may rejoice” and “I must mourn”. Each has its own subject and finite verb and could be a sentence alone; the comma between them is Douglass's choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a second subject with a verb of its own. A comma does not fuse two clauses into one.
Pair each subject with its finite verb. “May” and “must” belong to the verbs beside them, so they do not start clauses of their own.

questions.prompt: Lincoln: “The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here.” What is the grammatical function of “what we say here”?
hints: Ask: the world will little note what? The answer names the object.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'What we say here' is a noun clause that receives the action of 'note' and 'remember', so it is their object. The subject is 'the world'.

questions.onCorrect: It is what the world will note and remember, so it receives the action of both verbs and is their object.

misconceptions.feedback: The subject is the one doing the noting, which is “the world”. Ask what is noted, and you find the clause in question.
A complement follows a linking verb and describes the subject. “Note” and “remember” both act on something.

questions.prompt: “The vote was close, the motion failed.” What do editors call the fault in this sentence?
hints: Look at what separates the two halves, and at whether each half could stand alone.
The name pairs the mark with a word from rope-work and film editing.
Joining two lengths of rope or film end to end is called splicing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma splice: in edited prose a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.onCorrect: It is called a comma splice, from the sense of splicing two lengths of rope end to end, with the comma as the weak join.

misconceptions.feedback: A run-on sentence has no mark at all between the clauses. Here a comma is present, but it is too light to do the joining.

questions.prompt: Douglass: “To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.” Which verb is understood but not repeated in the second and third clauses?
hints: Read the first clause, then lend its verb to the second.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Is': each later clause means 'your boasted liberty is an unholy license'. The comma marks where the verb was left out.

questions.onCorrect: The verb is “is”: your boasted liberty is an unholy license, and the semicolon marks the place where the repeated verb has been dropped.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the things the clauses describe. Look for the small linking word in the first clause that the other two borrow.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
hints: Test the words before each colon: could they stand as a sentence?

acceptedIdeas: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A colon needs a complete clause before it, and what follows should explain or specify. Only the first sentence meets both conditions.

choices.label: The verdict was clear: the motion had failed by two votes.
The reasons were: cost and delay.
The motion: failed by two votes.

questions.onCorrect: The words before the colon, “The verdict was clear”, form a complete clause, and what follows explains them. A colon needs that complete clause in front of it.

misconceptions.feedback: “The motion” cannot stand alone, so the colon interrupts a clause instead of following one.
Look at the words before the colon. “The reasons were” does not make a complete clause, and the colon cuts the verb off from what it needs.

questions.prompt: Repair “It was late, we left” by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction that states cause and result. Which word do you add?
hints: The second clause is the result of the first. Which short word introduces a result?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'So': 'It was late, so we left.' 'And' would join the clauses without naming the cause.

questions.onCorrect: “So” joins the two clauses and states that leaving was the result of the lateness: “It was late, so we left.”

misconceptions.feedback: “And” would join them but say only that both things happened. You want the word that marks one as the result of the other.
“But” sets a clause against another. Here leaving follows from the lateness, so you need a word of result.

questions.prompt: Douglass writes “You may rejoice, I must mourn.” Keeping the comma, which coordinating conjunction would make this standard edited prose while keeping the contrast?
hints: Choose the conjunction that sets one clause against the other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'But' or 'yet': 'You may rejoice, but I must mourn.' Both name the contrast; 'and' would flatten it.

questions.onCorrect: “But” (or “yet”) keeps the contrast and repairs the splice: “You may rejoice, but I must mourn.” “And” would flatten the opposition.

misconceptions.feedback: “And” joins but does not oppose. Douglass sets rejoicing against mourning, and the word has to keep that opposition.
“So” would say that mourning follows from the rejoicing, and the sentence says the opposite.

questions.prompt: How many independent clauses are in this sentence: “The hall was full; the speaker was late: his train had stopped outside the city.”?
hints: Find each subject with its finite verb.
Check whether any clause opens with a subordinator such as 'because' or 'when'.
Each mark here separates complete clauses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'The hall was full', 'the speaker was late' and 'his train had stopped outside the city'. The colon introduces the reason for the lateness.

questions.onCorrect: There are three: “The hall was full”, “the speaker was late” and “his train had stopped outside the city”. The semicolon and the colon each join complete clauses.

misconceptions.feedback: Find the subject and finite verb after each mark. The colon introduces a third complete clause, which gives the reason for the lateness.
Marks like the semicolon and colon do not fuse clauses into one; each clause keeps its own subject and verb.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is “The motion was rejected by the committee” in the active voice?
hints: Find the actor after “by” and make it the subject.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The committee rejected the motion.

choices.label: The committee was rejecting the motion.
Rejected by the committee was the motion.

questions.onCorrect: The committee is the actor, so it becomes the subject, and “was rejected” becomes the plain verb “rejected”. Seven words become five.

misconceptions.feedback: The words have moved, but the motion still comes first and the committee is still not the subject, so the sentence leads with the thing acted on.
“Was rejecting” keeps a form of “be” and turns the rejection into something in progress; the active past is simply “rejected”.
The motion is still the subject and “by” still marks the committee, so the sentence is passive with its words reordered.

questions.prompt: Rewrite “Mistakes were made by the finance office” in the active voice. What becomes the subject?
hints: Find the 'by' phrase: whoever sits inside it performed the action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The finance office made mistakes.' The actor, hidden in the 'by' phrase, moves into the subject position.

questions.onCorrect: “The finance office made mistakes.” Once the actor leads, the sentence says who made them, and it loses two words.

misconceptions.feedback: “Mistakes” is the subject of the passive, which is the thing acted on. In the active the doer comes first.

questions.prompt: Unbury the verbs in “The committee made a decision to conduct a review of the policy”: “made a decision” becomes “decided”, and “conduct a review of” becomes “review”. How many words does the revision save?
hints: Count the words in the original sentence.
Write out the revision and count it.
Subtract the revised count from the original count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve words become seven: 'The committee decided to review the policy.' Five are saved.

questions.onCorrect: Twelve words become seven, “The committee decided to review the policy”, so five are saved. Each buried verb gave up several words.

misconceptions.feedback: Seven is the length of the revision. The question asks how many words you save, which is the difference.
That counts the saving from only one of the two replacements. Count the original sentence and the revision, then subtract.

questions.prompt: Cut the padding from “In my personal opinion, it is basically true that the final outcome depends on the weather.” Which sentence is left?
hints: Take each phrase out in turn and ask whether the sentence loses anything.

acceptedIdeas: The outcome depends on the weather.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The outcome depends on the weather.

choices.label: It is true that the final outcome depends on the weather.
The final outcome depends on the weather.
The outcome depends on the weather.
In my opinion, the final outcome depends on the weather.

questions.onCorrect: Six words are left. The frame adds nothing the reader would not assume, “personal” and “basically” add nothing to it, and an outcome is already final.

misconceptions.feedback: An outcome is the final result by definition, so “final” repeats what “outcome” already says and can go.
“It is true that” is a frame: the reader takes the statement as true unless told otherwise, so it adds length and no meaning, and “final” repeats what “outcome” says.
A statement you make is already your opinion, so the frame can go without the sentence losing anything, and so can “final”, since an outcome is already final.

questions.prompt: “The budget was approved by the council in March.” How many words does the active version save?
hints: Put the council in the subject position.
Write the active sentence and count it.
Subtract the active count from the passive count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine words become seven: 'The council approved the budget in March.' Two are saved.

questions.onCorrect: The active version, “The council approved the budget in March”, has seven words against nine, so it saves two.

misconceptions.feedback: Seven is the length of the active sentence. The question asks for the saving, which is the difference.
Two words drop out, “was” and “by”. The council, the budget and the date all stay.

questions.prompt: “An investigation of the causes was carried out by the board.” Which verb is buried inside the noun “investigation”?
hints: Remove the noun ending '-ation' and rebuild the verb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Investigate': 'The board investigated the causes' turns the noun back into a verb and the board into the subject.

questions.onCorrect: The verb is “investigate”. “The board investigated the causes” says the same in five words rather than ten.

misconceptions.feedback: “Carried out” is the weak verb that props up the noun. The buried verb is the action the noun names.

questions.prompt: Three statements: “Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.” “The bridge should close to lorries.” “A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.” Which is the claim?
hints: Ask which statement the others are there to support.
The claim is the one the arguer wants you to accept, and it need not come first.

acceptedIdeas: The bridge should close to lorries.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The bridge should close to lorries' is the conclusion the other two statements are offered to support.

choices.label: The bridge should close to lorries.
Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.

questions.onCorrect: “The bridge should close to lorries” is what the writer wants you to accept, and the other two statements exist to support it.

misconceptions.feedback: The cracks are a fact offered as a reason, which makes them grounds. The claim is the statement those facts are meant to support.
That is a general rule about damaged structures. It connects the facts to the conclusion rather than being the conclusion itself.

questions.prompt: Grounds: “The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.” Claim: “The defendant handled the knife.” What is Toulmin's name for the unstated rule “Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it”?
hints: The element authorises the step from evidence to conclusion; the same word names a document that authorises a search.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant: the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

questions.onCorrect: It is the warrant, the general rule that allows the move from these grounds to this claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The grounds are the fact already stated, the fingerprints. The rule that makes that fact count as a reason has a different name.
The claim is the conclusion, that the defendant handled the knife. The unstated rule has its own name.

questions.prompt: In “Harriet will probably win, unless rain keeps her supporters at home”, which single word is the qualifier?
hints: Find the word that measures how confident the claim is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Probably' limits the force of the claim; 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home' is the rebuttal, the condition under which it fails.

questions.onCorrect: “Probably” says how strongly the claim is made, while “unless rain keeps her supporters at home” gives the condition under which it fails.

misconceptions.feedback: “Unless” opens the rebuttal, the condition under which the claim fails. The qualifier is the word that measures how confident the claim is.
“Win” is the heart of the claim itself. Look for a word that tells you how strongly it is asserted.

questions.prompt: Four statements: “Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.” “Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.” “The price should return to its old level.” “Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.” Which is the warrant?
hints: Find the claim first: the statement the others support.
Find the observed fact; that is the grounds.
The warrant is a general rule rather than a particular fact.

acceptedIdeas: Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.

choices.label: Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.
The price should return to its old level.

questions.onCorrect: It is a general rule that links the fall in sales, the grounds, to the conclusion about price, the claim. The “unless” statement is the rebuttal.

misconceptions.feedback: The fall in sales is an observed fact, which makes it the grounds. The warrant is a general rule, not a particular figure.
This is what the writer wants you to accept, so it is the claim.
This begins with “unless”, so it states a condition under which the claim fails. That is the rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Four statements: “The museum should open late every Thursday.” “A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.” “Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.” “The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.” Which supplies the grounds?
hints: Find the statement the others support.
Grounds are particular observed facts, not general rules.

acceptedIdeas: Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.

choices.label: Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

questions.onCorrect: The doubled attendance is the observed fact offered as a reason, so it is the grounds. The opening late is the claim, the rule about staffing cost the warrant, and the short trial a rebuttal.

misconceptions.feedback: This is what the writer wants you to accept, which makes it the claim. Grounds are the facts offered in its support.
This is a general rule about changes that double attendance, and that makes it the warrant.
This limits the argument by pointing out a weakness, which makes it a rebuttal.

questions.prompt: A writer supports the warrant “Damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads” by citing the national bridge inspection code. In Toulmin's model, what is that support called?
hints: The support is aimed at the rule, not at the conclusion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Backing: support for the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

questions.onCorrect: Support for the warrant itself is called backing. Grounds support the claim, whereas backing stands behind the rule that links them.

misconceptions.feedback: Grounds are the facts offered for the claim. The inspection code supports the rule, and that is aimed at the warrant.
A qualifier is a word such as “probably” that limits the force of the claim. Citing a code does not do that.

questions.prompt: Douglass tells his Rochester audience, “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.” His right to say it rests on his own life as a man who had escaped slavery. Which of Aristotle's appeals is he relying on?
hints: The Greek word is the root of 'ethics'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: the persuasive force of the speaker's character and credibility.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos: Douglass's authority comes from who he is and what he has lived through, so his audience has to take seriously what he says about the holiday.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos works on the audience's feelings. Here the force comes from the speaker's standing, from who he is.
Logos is an appeal through reasoning. The line states no argument; it draws its force from the speaker himself.

questions.prompt: “The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.” Which appeal does this sentence chiefly make?
hints: The Greek root also gives English 'sympathy'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: the appeal to the audience's emotions, here pity and shame.

questions.onCorrect: Pathos: the image sets a picture of suffering beside a picture of comfort, and it asks the audience to feel the difference.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos draws on the speaker's character and standing. This sentence works through a picture put before the audience.
Logos moves from reasons to a conclusion. This sentence offers no reasons; it sets a picture before the audience.

questions.prompt: Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg in November 1863. “Four score and seven years ago” points back to which year?
hints: A score is twenty.
Four score and seven is four twenties plus seven.
Subtract that number of years from the year of the speech.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7 = 87, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

questions.onCorrect: Four score and seven is 4 × 20 + 7, which makes 87 years, and 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

misconceptions.feedback: Eighty-seven is how many years Lincoln means. The question asks for the year, so subtract it from 1863.
That counts back only four score, which is 80 years. The seven makes the total 87 before you subtract from 1863.

questions.prompt: Douglass delivered his attack on slavery at a celebration of American independence, the day after the Fourth of July, and made the holiday itself part of his case. Which appeal does that choice of day use?
hints: It is the term often added to Aristotle's three appeals, and it means the opportune moment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Kairos: the timeliness of a speech, the fit between argument and occasion.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos names the fit between a speech and its occasion. Douglass chose a day of national celebration to show what the celebration left out.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the three appeals Aristotle named. The term wanted here names the timing and the occasion, and it is usually added as a fourth.

questions.prompt: Lincoln says the war is “testing whether that nation, or any nation so conceived and so dedicated, can long endure.” He reasons from the nation's founding premise to what the war puts at stake. Which appeal is this chiefly?
hints: Look for the appeal named after the Greek for 'word' or 'reason'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Logos: an appeal through reasoning from premise to consequence.

questions.onCorrect: Logos: Lincoln starts from the founding premise and shows what the war puts at stake, so the force of the sentence comes from its reasoning.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos would lean on the speaker's standing. This sentence moves from a premise to what follows from it.
Pathos would stir the audience's feelings. This sentence reasons from a premise to its consequence.

questions.prompt: A charity letter opens: “As a children's nurse for twenty years, I have seen what a missed vaccination can do.” Which appeal does the opening clause make first?
hints: Look at what the opening clause tells you about the writer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ethos: 'As a children's nurse for twenty years' establishes the writer's experience and credibility before anything else.

questions.onCorrect: The clause tells the reader who is writing and for how long, so it establishes the writer's credibility. That is ethos, and any picture of harm comes after it.

misconceptions.feedback: Pathos would put a picture before the reader's feelings. The opening clause is about the writer, and the feeling comes later.
Kairos concerns fitting a speech to its moment. The opening clause tells us nothing about timing; it establishes who is writing.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities (1859): “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.” How many times does “it was” open a clause in this extract?
hints: Split the extract at each comma.
Mark the first two words of each clause.
Count the clauses that open the same way.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. The repeated opening is anaphora; in the full sentence Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses.

questions.onCorrect: Four. Dickens keeps the same opening going for ten clauses in the full sentence, and each repetition makes the contrast that follows it stand out.

misconceptions.feedback: Count past the first comma: “it was” starts every clause of the extract, not only the first two.
You may have counted the words rather than the openings. Count how many clauses begin with “it was”.
Split the extract at each comma, and check the first two words of every part.

questions.prompt: Lincoln sets “what we say here” against “what they did here”. Name the figure.
hints: The Greek name means 'setting against'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Antithesis: contrasting ideas placed in parallel form, here saying against doing and 'we' against 'they'.

questions.onCorrect: Antithesis: saying is set against doing and “we” against “they”, in clauses of the same shape, so that the contrast can be seen at once.

misconceptions.feedback: Anaphora repeats the opening words of successive clauses. Here the clauses begin differently, and it is the opposed ideas that are balanced.
Chiasmus reverses the order of its terms. These two halves keep the same order, which is why the figure is another one.

questions.prompt: Douglass, 1845: “You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.” Name the figure.
hints: The name comes from the Greek letter chi, shaped like an X.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus (strictly antimetabole, since the same words return): A B, then B A.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole, since the same words return: man and slave in the first half become slave and man in the second.

misconceptions.feedback: The terms are certainly opposed, but the figure is named for the way they return: in reverse order, like the strokes of an X.
Anaphora repeats the opening of each clause. Here the two halves begin alike, but what is notable is that the terms swap places.

questions.prompt: “Government of the people, by the people, for the people.” Which of the figures in this lesson does Lincoln's phrase form?
hints: The Greek prefix for three is joined to the word for a clause or limb.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three prepositional phrases sharing one noun.

questions.onCorrect: A tricolon: three parallel members in a row, here three short phrases that share the same noun and differ only in the preposition.

misconceptions.feedback: The repeated word does begin the members, but the figure that names a series of exactly three parallel members is a different one.

questions.prompt: Douglass: “your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license; your national greatness, swelling vanity.” Which figure does the repeated opening “your” create?
hints: Repetition at the start of successive clauses has a name from the Greek for 'carrying back'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Anaphora: repetition at the start of successive clauses, here pointing each charge at the audience.

questions.onCorrect: Anaphora: the repeated “your” starts each clause, and it points every charge back at the audience.

misconceptions.feedback: There are three parts, but the repeated opening is what the question asks about, and that has a name of its own.
Nothing is set against anything in the repeated opening. What is repeated is a single word at the start of each clause.

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant “Fair is foul, and foul is fair.” Which figure is this?
hints: Look at the order of the two repeated words in each half.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus: fair, foul / foul, fair. The reversal suits a play in which appearances invert.

questions.onCorrect: Chiasmus: “fair, foul” returns as “foul, fair”. The reversal suits a play in which appearances turn into their opposites.

misconceptions.feedback: Anaphora repeats the opening of clauses. Here the repeated words swap places instead.
A tricolon needs three parallel members. This line has two halves, with the same two words in reverse order.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Sonnet 18, line 1: “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?”
hints: Say the line slowly and tap once for each vowel sound.
'Compare' and 'summer's' have two syllables each.
Every other word has one syllable; add them up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: shall / I / com / pare / thee / to / a / sum / mer's / day.

questions.onCorrect: Ten: shall / I / com / pare / thee / to / a / sum / mer's / day. Only “compare” and “summer's” have two syllables.

misconceptions.feedback: You have counted the words. “Compare” and “summer's” each hold two syllables, so the syllables outnumber the words.
One of the two-syllable words has been counted once. Tap out each vowel sound in turn.
One word has been counted for too many syllables. Only “compare” and “summer's” have two.

questions.prompt: In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables. Counting from the first syllable, on which syllable does the third beat fall?
hints: List the syllable positions that carry beats.
The first beat falls on the second syllable.
Each further beat comes two syllables later.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

questions.onCorrect: The beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, so the third is on syllable 6. In “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”, that is the first syllable of “darling”.

misconceptions.feedback: Three is the position of the beat in the list of beats. The question asks which syllable of the line it falls on.
Odd-numbered syllables are the weak ones in an iamb, since each iamb puts its strong syllable second. List the even-numbered syllables and take the third.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Sonnet 116, line 6: “That looks on tempests and is never shaken”?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Tempests', 'never' and 'shaken' have two syllables each.
Notice what follows the last beat on 'sha-'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eleven. '-ken' is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat on 'sha-': a feminine ending.

questions.onCorrect: Eleven. “Shaken” ends with a weak syllable after the last beat on “sha-”, which makes the line one syllable longer than a regular line of ten.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the two-syllable words: “tempests”, “never” and “shaken”. Their second syllables bring the total above ten.
That counts the words with one syllable each. “Tempests”, “never” and “shaken” have two syllables each.

questions.prompt: The witches in Macbeth chant “Double, double, toil and trouble”: DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Name this foot.
hints: Its Greek name means 'running'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter.

questions.onCorrect: The trochee: a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one, the reverse of the iamb.

misconceptions.feedback: An iamb rises, from weak to strong. In this line each foot starts with the stressed syllable and falls away.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Emily Dickinson's “That perches in the soul”?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Perches' has two syllables.
Count the remaining one-syllable words and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: that / per / ches / in / the / soul. Three iambs make iambic trimeter.

questions.onCorrect: Six: that / per / ches / in / the / soul. Only “perches” has two syllables, and three iambs make a line of six.

misconceptions.feedback: You have counted the words. “Perches” has two syllables, so the syllables outnumber the words.
No word here has more than two syllables, and only “perches” has two.

questions.prompt: A line has four iambic feet, as in Dickinson's “And sings the tune without the words”. Name its metre: iambic what?
hints: The Greek prefix for four comes before '-meter'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Iambic tetrameter: four iambs, eight syllables.

questions.onCorrect: Tetrameter: the Greek prefix means four, so the line holds four iambs and eight syllables.

misconceptions.feedback: Pentameter has five feet. This line has four, one fewer.
Trimeter has three feet. This line has four.

questions.prompt: In “When to the sessions of sweet silent thought”, how many words begin with the s sound?
hints: Read the line aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore s sounds in the middle or at the end of words.
Check the nouns and adjectives one by one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'sessions', 'sweet' and 'silent'. The hushed s sounds suit a line about silent thought.

questions.onCorrect: Three: “sessions”, “sweet” and “silent”. The hushed s sounds suit a line about silent thought.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the last word: “thought” begins with the th sound, which is different from s.
Read the line once more and listen to how each word starts. Three words open with the same hissing sound.

questions.prompt: In Keats's “Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness”, how many words contain the long vowel heard in “bride”?
hints: Listen to vowel sounds rather than letters: 'still' has a short vowel.
Say 'quietness' slowly: qui-et-ness.
Count every word whose vowel matches the one in the model word, including that word itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'bride' and 'quietness' (qui-). 'Still' and 'unravish'd' have the short vowel of 'sit'.

questions.onCorrect: Two: “bride” and “quietness”, whose first syllable has the same sound. “Still” and “unravish'd” have the short vowel of “sit”.

misconceptions.feedback: Say “quietness” slowly: qui-et-ness. Its first syllable has the same vowel as “bride”.
“Still” and “unravish'd” contain the letter i, but their vowel is the short sound of “sit”. Listen rather than look.

questions.prompt: Burns: “O my Luve's like a red, red rose.” Name the figure.
hints: The figure announces itself as a comparison; its name shares a root with 'similar'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.onCorrect: A simile: “like” announces the comparison, so the reader is told that Burns's love and a rose are being set side by side.

misconceptions.feedback: A metaphor would say that she is a rose, with no word to announce the comparison. Here “like” announces it.

questions.prompt: In Dickinson's “Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul”, hope is pictured as a creature. Which creature is implied?
hints: It has feathers and perches, and in the next lines it sings.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bird: the feathers, the perching and later the singing belong to it, and the second stanza names 'the little bird'.

questions.onCorrect: A bird: feathers, perching and, later in the poem, singing all belong to one. Dickinson never writes the word in these lines.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at what hope is given: feathers, and a place to perch. Which creature has both?

questions.prompt: Wordsworth: “I wandered lonely as a Cloud.” Name the figure.
hints: Look for the word that announces a comparison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A simile: 'as' makes the comparison between the speaker and the cloud explicit.

questions.onCorrect: A simile: “as” makes the comparison between the speaker and the cloud explicit.

misconceptions.feedback: A metaphor would say that the speaker was a cloud. This line uses “as” to announce the comparison instead.

questions.prompt: Romeo says of Juliet at her window, “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!” Which statement is accurate?
hints: Is there a 'like' or an 'as'?

acceptedIdeas: It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A metaphor: Romeo identifies Juliet with the sun rather than comparing her with 'like' or 'as'.

choices.label: It is a simile, because two things are compared
It is alliteration on the s sound
It is a metaphor: Juliet is identified with the sun

questions.onCorrect: Romeo does not say that Juliet is like the sun; he says she is the sun. With no “like” or “as”, the comparison is carried by the plain verb “is”, and that is what makes it a metaphor.

misconceptions.feedback: A simile would carry a word such as “like” or “as”. Romeo has no such word; he says she is the sun.
Repeated sounds are not what is at work in the line. The comparison of Juliet with the sun is the point.

questions.prompt: A Shakespearean sonnet rhymes ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. How many different rhyme sounds does that scheme use?
hints: Each letter stands for one rhyme sound.
List the letters without repeats.
Count the distinct letters from A onward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven, A to G: three quatrains bring two new rhymes each, and the couplet adds one.

questions.onCorrect: Seven, A to G. Each of the three quatrains brings two new sounds, and the couplet adds one more.

misconceptions.feedback: Fourteen is the number of lines. Each letter stands for a sound, and a sound is reused on several lines.
List the distinct letters from A onwards. The scheme stops one letter earlier than you have counted.
The three quatrains give six sounds, but the couplet introduces one more.

questions.prompt: The octave of Milton's sonnet on his blindness ends its lines on spent, wide, hide, bent, present, chide, denied and prevent. How many different rhyme sounds does it use?
hints: Give “spent” the letter A, and give each new sound the next letter.
A word that rhymes with an earlier one takes that word's letter.
Count the different letters you have used.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: A (spent, bent, present, prevent) and B (wide, hide, chide, deny'd).

questions.onCorrect: Two: A on spent, bent, present and prevent, and B on wide, hide, chide and denied. The same two sounds are reused four times each.

misconceptions.feedback: Eight is the number of lines. A letter stands for a sound, and sounds are repeated.
Each sound is used four times in the octave, which is how many times it recurs rather than how many sounds there are.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 29, lines 8 to 10, run: “With what I most enjoy contented least; / Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising, / Haply I think on thee, and then my state”. At which line does the poem turn from despair to consolation?
hints: Find the first word that changes the direction of the argument.
Look at the opening of the third quatrain.
Count the lines down to that word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 9: 'Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising'. 'Yet' turns the poem after two quatrains of complaint.

questions.onCorrect: At line 9: “Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising” turns the poem after two quatrains of complaint, and the next line brings the thought of the beloved.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 10 is where the consolation arrives, with “Haply I think on thee”. The turn comes a line earlier, with the word that changes direction.
Line 13 sits in the couplet, which here confirms the consolation. The turn itself comes at the opening of the third quatrain.

questions.prompt: Sonnet 130 spends its quatrains mocking conventional comparisons. At which line does it turn?
hints: Find the words that reverse the poem's direction.
Look where the closing couplet begins.
Count the lines in the three quatrains, then add one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 13: 'And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare'. The couplet carries the turn.

questions.onCorrect: At line 13: “And yet by heaven, I think my love as rare”. The couplet carries the turn, and the “yet” announces it.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 9 is where many sonnets turn, but this one holds its turn back until the couplet.
Line 14 completes the thought. The turn begins one line earlier, with the words that reverse the poem's direction.

questions.prompt: Milton turns inside line 8: “I fondly ask. But Patience, to prevent / That murmur, soon replies”. Which quality, spoken of as if it were a person, answers the speaker?
hints: Read the words after 'But' in line 8.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Patience: it interrupts the complaint and answers it in the sestet, ending 'They also serve who only stand and waite.'

questions.onCorrect: Patience answers, and the sestet gives its reply in the speaker's place. The turn comes in the middle of the line, at “But”, rather than at the line's start.

misconceptions.feedback: God is named in the reply, but he is not the one who speaks. Look at the word after “But” for the quality that answers.

questions.prompt: Which describes the final two lines of a Shakespearean sonnet?
hints: The scheme ends with a repeated letter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rhyming couplet, GG, often carrying the turn or the answer to the quatrains.

questions.onCorrect: They form a rhyming couplet, GG, and often carry the turn or the answer to the three quatrains that precede them.

misconceptions.feedback: A tercet rhyming CDE belongs to the Italian form's closing sestet. The Shakespearean form ends on a pair.
The final two lines rhyme with each other, and the scheme ends GG.

questions.prompt: Austen opens Emma (1815): “Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.” In which grammatical person is this narration?
hints: Does the narrator say 'I', or describe Emma from outside?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third person: the narrator names Emma and refers to her as 'she', standing outside the story.

questions.onCorrect: Third person: the narrator names Emma and refers to her from outside the story, with no “I” anywhere in the sentence.

misconceptions.feedback: A first-person narrator would say “I” or “we”, as the narrator of the Poe passage does. Here the narrator stays outside and refers to Emma by name.
Second person would address the reader as “you”. This sentence describes Emma from outside.

questions.prompt: Pride and Prejudice (1813) opens: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” Whose view does the sentence express?
hints: No character has yet appeared when the sentence is spoken.

acceptedIdeas: The narrator, voicing a neighbourhood's assumption with irony
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The narrator states the assumption as if it were universal; the next paragraph shows it belongs to families with daughters to marry.

choices.label: Elizabeth Bennet, in her private thoughts
The narrator, voicing a neighbourhood's assumption with irony
Mr Bennet, speaking to his wife

questions.onCorrect: It is the narrator's voice, stating a neighbourhood's assumption as if it were a universal truth. The next paragraph shows that the assumption belongs to families with daughters to marry.

misconceptions.feedback: Mr Bennet has not yet spoken, and no character has appeared when the sentence is said. It comes from the narrator.
Elizabeth is not yet on the scene, and the sentence is not marked as a private thought. It belongs to the narrator.

questions.prompt: After Mr Elton's proposal Austen writes: “Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!” Which technique does the second sentence use?
hints: Compare it with 'She thought that it was a wretched business'. Which part has been dropped, and what does that make the reported thought?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse, also called free indirect style or speech: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice.

questions.onCorrect: Free indirect discourse: the narrator's grammar carries Emma's own exclamation, so we hear her voice without a reporting verb.

misconceptions.feedback: Direct speech would use quotation marks and the character's own pronouns. This sentence keeps the narrator's person and tense.
Plain indirect speech would include a reporting verb, as in “she thought that it was a wretched business”. This sentence drops it.

questions.prompt: Here are three sentences from Emma, chapter 16. Which is free indirect discourse?
hints: Direct speech sits inside quotation marks.
Plain narration reports actions from outside.
Look for a character's exclamation in the third person.

acceptedIdeas: How she could have been so deceived!
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How she could have been so deceived!

choices.label: “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
How she could have been so deceived!

questions.onCorrect: It is Emma's exclamation in the third person and past tense, with no reporting verb. The first sentence is direct speech, in quotation marks, and the second is narration.

misconceptions.feedback: This sits in quotation marks and uses “I”, which makes it direct speech.
This reports what happens from outside, which is plain narration.

questions.prompt: Turn the direct thought “I have been a fool” into free indirect discourse about Emma. Which pronoun replaces “I”?
hints: Free indirect discourse uses the narrator's grammatical person, not the character's.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'She had been a fool!' The person shifts to the third and the tense moves back, but the exclamation stays Emma's.

questions.onCorrect: “She”: the sentence moves into the narrator's third person and past tense, as in “She had been a fool!”, while the exclamation stays Emma's.

misconceptions.feedback: The thought is Emma's, so the pronoun that fits a woman in the narrator's third person is the one to use.
Free indirect discourse uses the narrator's grammatical person and not the character's own.

questions.prompt: Which feature most reliably marks free indirect discourse?
hints: Think about what is missing compared with 'she thought that'.

acceptedIdeas: A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse keeps the narrator's person and tense but drops the reporting verb, so the character's idiom enters the narration directly.

choices.label: A first-person narrator addressing the reader
