Quotation marks around a character's words
A character's own exclamations and idiom in third-person past tense, with no reporting verb

questions.onCorrect: A character's own exclamation or idiom in the narrator's third person and past tense, with no reporting verb, is the mark. The thought arrives without being announced.

misconceptions.feedback: Quotation marks belong to direct speech. Free indirect discourse drops them.
A first-person narrator is a different way of telling a story. Free indirect discourse sits inside third-person narration.

questions.prompt: In the eight lines shown from Antony's funeral speech, how many times is Brutus called “an honourable man”?
hints: Look for the exact phrase with the singular 'man'.
'All honourable men' refers to the conspirators as a group; leave it out.
Count each line that applies the phrase to Brutus, including the one that calls him 'he'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so the praise turns into accusation: verbal irony.

questions.onCorrect: Four. Each repetition follows evidence against the charge of ambition, so the praise turns into accusation. That is verbal irony.

misconceptions.feedback: “All honourable men” refers to the conspirators as a group and uses a different phrase. Count only the lines that call Brutus himself “an honourable man”.
One of the repetitions has been missed. Check the first line and the last, as well as the middle ones.
Eight is the number of lines. Count only the lines in which Brutus himself is called “an honourable man”.

questions.prompt: Romeo, in the tomb, believes Juliet is dead; the audience knows she has taken a sleeping potion and will wake. Which kind of irony does the scene create?
hints: It is named after the form in which it is most at home: plays.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience's knowledge exceeds the character's, so his words carry a meaning he cannot hear.

questions.onCorrect: Dramatic irony: the audience's knowledge exceeds Romeo's, so his words about Juliet's beauty carry a meaning he cannot hear.

misconceptions.feedback: Verbal irony needs a speaker who means the opposite of what he says. Romeo means every word; it is the audience's knowledge that changes what they mean.
Situational irony lies in an outcome that reverses an intention. Here the point is what the audience knows that Romeo does not.

questions.prompt: Romeo steps between Mercutio and Tybalt to stop the fight, and Tybalt's thrust under his arm kills Mercutio. Which kind of irony is this?
hints: The irony lies in how events turn out, not in what anyone says or knows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Situational irony: the outcome reverses the intention that produced it.

questions.onCorrect: Situational irony: the outcome reverses the intention that produced it. Romeo's peace-making is what makes the death possible.

misconceptions.feedback: Dramatic irony depends on the audience knowing more than a character. Here the irony lies in how the event turns out.
Verbal irony is in what someone says. The irony here is in an outcome, which is the reverse of what Romeo intended.

questions.prompt: Poe's narrator insists he is sane while describing a murder in frantic, broken sentences. What kind of narrator is he?
hints: It is the opposite of a narrator whose word you can trust.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An unreliable narrator: the telling itself, with its dashes and protests, gives evidence against what it claims.

questions.onCorrect: An unreliable narrator: the telling itself, with its dashes and protests, gives the reader evidence against what the narrator claims.

misconceptions.feedback: An omniscient narrator knows everything and can be trusted to tell it. This narrator gives us reasons to doubt him.
Irony is the gap between what is said and what is meant. The term wanted names the kind of narrator whose account cannot be trusted.

questions.prompt: Austen's narrator calls it “a truth universally acknowledged” that a rich single man “must be in want of a wife”; the novel shows it is the families who want the man. Which kind of irony does the sentence use: dramatic, situational or verbal?
hints: The irony lives in the wording of a statement.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the statement says one thing and means its reverse.

questions.onCorrect: Verbal irony: the narrator states the assumption as a universal truth and means something close to its opposite, that the neighbours believe it for their own ends.

misconceptions.feedback: Dramatic irony needs the audience to know something that a character does not. Here a narrator says one thing and means another.
Situational irony lies in an outcome that reverses an intention. This sentence is about how the narrator words a claim.

questions.prompt: In a play, the audience has watched a character poison the wine. The host then raises a glass and toasts his guest's long life. Which kind of irony is at work?
hints: Ask who knows about the poison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dramatic irony: the audience knows about the poison and the host does not, so his toast means something he cannot hear.

questions.onCorrect: Dramatic irony: the audience knows about the poison and the host does not, so his toast means something he cannot hear.

misconceptions.feedback: Situational irony needs an outcome that turns against an intention. Here the point is what the audience knows that the host does not.
The host means what he says, so the irony does not come from saying the opposite. It comes from what the audience knows.

questions.prompt: Romeo and Juliet has five acts. In which act does the climax fall in Freytag's scheme, the high point after which the action turns against the lovers?
hints: Think about where the lovers' luck stops climbing.
Which act holds Tybalt's death and Romeo's banishment?

acceptedIdeas: Act 3, near the middle of the play
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Act 3, near the middle of the play

choices.label: Act 1, where the lovers first meet
Act 3, near the middle of the play

questions.onCorrect: Act 3. Mercutio and Tybalt die and Romeo is banished, and from that point the lovers' luck runs downhill to the tomb.

misconceptions.feedback: Act 1 is where the lovers meet and the conflict begins, and their fortunes go on rising through the balcony and the wedding after it.
Act 5 is the catastrophe, the end of the fall. The high point comes earlier, once the lovers' luck stops climbing.

questions.prompt: A novel's first chapter shows a fishing village, its harbour master and his two daughters, before the storm that sets the plot going has arrived. Which part of Freytag's pyramid is this chapter?
hints: It comes first and explains the situation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The exposition, Freytag's 'Einleitung' or introduction.

questions.onCorrect: The exposition, which Freytag called the Einleitung, or introduction. It sets out what the audience needs before the conflict can start.

misconceptions.feedback: The climax is the high point, which comes much later. The part wanted comes first and sets the scene.
The rising action builds the conflict once it has begun. The part wanted comes before the conflict starts.

questions.prompt: The figure gives eight scenes of Romeo and Juliet, each opening and closing with a value for the lovers, + or −. A scene turns when its closing value differs from its opening value. How many of the eight scenes turn?
hints: Read each scene's opening and closing sign.
A scene that opens + and closes + does not turn.
Count the scenes whose two signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Five: 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold their value.

questions.onCorrect: Five: 1.5, 3.1, 3.5, 4.1 and 5.1. The balcony, the wedding and the tomb hold their value from start to finish.

misconceptions.feedback: Eight is the number of scenes. A scene turns only when its closing sign differs from its opening sign.
One turning scene has been missed. Compare the opening and closing sign of all eight.
Three is the number of scenes that hold a + from start to finish. Count the scenes whose signs differ instead.

questions.prompt: The diagram plots how high the action has climbed in each of six numbered scenes of a heist story. Which scene is the climax?
hints: Freytag's climax is the highest point of the pyramid.
Compare the heights of the scene markers.
Give the scene's number, counting from the left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there and every later scene descends.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4, the alarm: the action peaks there, and every later scene sits lower.

misconceptions.feedback: Scene 3 is still rising, since the next scene stands higher. The climax is the highest point.
Scene 5 comes after the peak, and the line is already falling there. Look for the tallest marker.

questions.prompt: In Freytag's scheme, what is the final part of a tragedy, in which the hero falls, called?
hints: The Greek word means an overturning.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The catastrophe, Freytag's 'Katastrophe'; in other plots the same position is called the denouement or resolution.

questions.onCorrect: The catastrophe, from a Greek word meaning an overturning. In other kinds of plot the same position is often called the denouement or resolution.

misconceptions.feedback: The climax is the high point at the middle of the pyramid. The part wanted is the last one, after the falling action.
The exposition opens the story. The part wanted closes a tragedy.

questions.prompt: Tybalt's death is the climax of Romeo and Juliet. Romeo's banishment follows it, and Juliet takes the Friar's potion in Act 4. Where do the banishment and the potion sit on Freytag's pyramid?
hints: Do they come before or after the climax?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Falling action: after the climax, events carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe.

questions.onCorrect: Both come after the climax and carry the lovers down towards the catastrophe in the tomb, so they belong to the falling action.

misconceptions.feedback: Rising action comes before the climax. These events follow Tybalt's death, so they sit on the other side of the peak.
The exposition opens the story, before the conflict begins. These events come after the climax.

questions.prompt: “The window was broken by Sam.” Say it so that Sam comes first. What happens to the sentence?
hints: Write the sentence out starting with “Sam”.

acceptedIdeas: It loses “was” and “by” and becomes four words long
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It loses “was” and “by” and becomes four words long

choices.label: It needs an extra word to show that Sam did it
It loses “was” and “by” and becomes four words long
It keeps the same six words in a new order

questions.onCorrect: “Sam broke the window” has four words. Putting the actor first turns “was broken” back into “broke” and leaves “by” with no work to do.

misconceptions.feedback: Moving Sam to the front changes the verb as well: “was broken” becomes “broke”, and “by” drops out, so two words go.
In the active sentence Sam's place at the front already shows who acted, so no word is needed to mark it, and “by” can go.

questions.prompt: In “The pitch was flooded by the storm”, which word names the actor?
hints: Look inside the “by” phrase.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: storm

questions.onCorrect: The storm did the flooding. In the passive the actor moves into a “by” phrase, and the receiver becomes the subject.

misconceptions.feedback: The pitch receives the action. Find the one that does it.
“Flooded” is the action itself. Ask who or what did it.

questions.prompt: Why does the active version read as stronger?

acceptedIdeas: The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The actor leads and the verb is shorter.

choices.label: It is longer, so it carries more detail.
The reader meets the actor first, and the verb is shorter.

questions.onCorrect: The actor leads and the verb is direct, so the sentence says who did what in fewer words.

misconceptions.feedback: It is shorter, not longer. The extra words in the passive carry nothing.
Not always. The passive suits cases where the actor is unknown or does not matter.

questions.prompt: “A review of the rules was undertaken by the staff.” Which sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb?
hints: Two things have to change: who leads, and where the action sits.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The staff reviewed the rules.

choices.label: The staff undertook a review of the rules.
The rules were reviewed by the staff.

questions.onCorrect: “The staff reviewed the rules” has the actor as its subject and the action in a plain verb. The other versions keep the review buried or put the staff last.

misconceptions.feedback: The staff lead here, but “undertook a review of” still buries the action in a noun. The action has to be the verb itself.
That is a passive sentence, with the staff at the end behind “by”. The actor has to lead.

questions.prompt: Which noun buries the verb in “The board gave a refusal of the request”?
hints: Look for an action word that has become a noun.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: refusal

questions.onCorrect: “A refusal” is the action turned into a noun, and “gave” is a weak verb carrying it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Request” names what was refused. Find the noun that is really an action.
“Board” is the actor. The buried verb is hidden in an action noun.

questions.prompt: You are choosing a mountain guide. Which sentence makes you trust her most before she says anything else?
hints: Which sentence tells you something about the speaker herself?

acceptedIdeas: “I have led this route forty times.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her forty trips of the route earn trust.

choices.label: “I have led this route forty times.”

questions.onCorrect: Her record is what earns trust. A speaker's own experience can persuade before any argument begins.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a guess about the weather. It tells you nothing about her.
That is a fact anyone could state. It says nothing about her experience.

questions.prompt: “Because the budget has doubled while results have not, the programme should be reviewed.” Which of the three appeals is at work: ethos, pathos or logos?
hints: Does the sentence reason, or does it move the audience?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: logos

questions.onCorrect: The sentence gives a reason and draws a conclusion from it, which is reasoning, and reasoning is what logos names.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing here tells us who the speaker is or why to trust them. The sentence offers a reason instead.
The sentence tries to stir no feeling. It reasons from a fact about the budget to a conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why does “As a lifelong farmer” count as ethos?

acceptedIdeas: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It tells the audience who is speaking and why to trust her.

choices.label: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
It gives a reason for the policy.

questions.onCorrect: Ethos works through the speaker's character and standing. Experience is part of what makes her believable.

misconceptions.feedback: It arouses no fear. It tells you who is speaking.
A reason would be an argument. This phrase only says who the speaker is.

questions.prompt: “Think of the families who lost everything in the flood.” Which appeal does the sentence rely on?
hints: What does the sentence ask the audience to imagine?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos

questions.onCorrect: The sentence asks the audience to picture people in distress, and the picture does the persuading. That is pathos.

misconceptions.feedback: Ethos would give us a reason to trust the speaker. This sentence is about the families, and it asks us to feel for them.
Logos would offer a reason. This sentence asks us to imagine instead of reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which best describes kairos?
hints: The word means the right moment.

acceptedIdeas: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fitting an argument to its moment and place.

choices.label: Arguing from a premise to a consequence.
Repeating a word at the start of clauses.
Fitting an argument to its moment and place.

questions.onCorrect: Kairos is the opportune moment: a speech fits its occasion and may use the place itself as evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a figure of repetition, not a proof. Kairos is about timing.
That describes reasoning, not timing.

questions.prompt: Your friend says “Get a dog: mine makes me so happy.” Which of these does she leave unsaid?
hints: Compare each statement with her exact words.
One statement is a belief that her advice relies on.

acceptedIdeas: What makes her happy will make you happy.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: What makes her happy will make you happy.

choices.label: What makes her happy will make you happy.

questions.onCorrect: She states the claim and the grounds aloud and leaves the rule that links them for you to supply, and that unstated rule is the part worth questioning.

misconceptions.feedback: “Get a dog” says this aloud, in the form of advice, and it is the claim she wants you to accept.
“Mine makes me so happy” says this aloud, and it is the reason she offers.

questions.prompt: “The pavement is wet, so it has rained.” Which words give the grounds?
hints: Which part can you check by looking?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: the pavement is wet

questions.onCorrect: The grounds are the observed fact. “It has rained” is the claim, and the link between them is the warrant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the conclusion drawn from the fact, so it is the claim. Find the fact itself.
That would be a general rule linking fact to conclusion. Grounds are the particular fact.

questions.prompt: Why is “forecasts are usually right” a warrant and not grounds?

acceptedIdeas: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a general rule linking the particular fact to the claim.

choices.label: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
It comes last in the sentence.

questions.onCorrect: A warrant is a general rule. Grounds are the particular fact it lets you rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: Position does not decide the role. Ask whether the statement is a fact or a rule.
A qualifier can sit in any statement. The question is what job the statement does.

questions.prompt: In “The tournament will almost certainly go ahead, unless the pitch floods”, which part is the rebuttal?
hints: Which part says when the claim would not hold?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unless the pitch floods

questions.onCorrect: “Unless the pitch floods” names a condition under which the claim would fail, and that is what a rebuttal does.

misconceptions.feedback: “Almost certainly” measures how strongly the claim is made, which makes it the qualifier.
“The tournament will go ahead” is the claim, the statement being qualified and then limited.

questions.prompt: In “Buses are usually on time, unless snow falls”, which word opens the rebuttal?
hints: Which word introduces what could stop the claim holding?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unless

questions.onCorrect: The rebuttal names the condition under which the claim would fail, and here it opens with “unless”.

misconceptions.feedback: “Usually” measures how often the claim holds. A rebuttal names what could defeat it.
That is part of the claim. A rebuttal limits it from outside.

questions.prompt: “The dog chases the ball.” Retell it as yesterday's story. Which word has to change?
hints: Say the sentence with “yesterday” at the start and listen for the word you have to alter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: chases

questions.onCorrect: Only “chases” becomes “chased”. The dog, the ball and both “the”s read the same at any time, which is why the word that moves is the one to look for.

misconceptions.feedback: “The” reads the same in “The dog chased the ball”, since a little word like this never changes with the time.
“Dog” names the one doing the chasing, and it stays “dog” whether the chasing happens today or yesterday.
“Ball” is what gets chased, and it keeps the same form at any time, while the word that says what happens has to move.

questions.prompt: Which word is the finite verb in “The old man walked home slowly”?
hints: Put the sentence into the present. Which word changes?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: walked

questions.onCorrect: “Walked” carries the tense. It would be “walks” in the present, and “the old man” is who does it.

misconceptions.feedback: “Old” describes the man and does not change with time. Find the word that would change in the present.
“Slowly” says how it happens. It stays the same in any tense.
“Home” names where he went. It stays the same in any tense.

questions.prompt: Why is “fierce” a complement and not an object?

acceptedIdeas: It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Was” links the subject to a description, so “fierce” is a complement.

choices.label: It is a single word, and objects need two.
It says what the subject is like, and nothing receives an action.
It is the last word in the clause.

questions.onCorrect: A complement says what the subject is or is like. An object receives the verb's action.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask whether the word receives an action or describes the subject.
Objects can be one word too, as in “shook the roof”. Ask what the word does.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a dependent clause?
hints: Which one would leave you waiting for the rest of the sentence?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: when the rain stopped

choices.label: The rain stopped and the sun came out

questions.onCorrect: “When” makes the clause lean on another one. It has a subject and a finite verb, but it leaves the reader waiting for more.

misconceptions.feedback: That could be a sentence on its own, so it is independent.
Both of its clauses could stand alone. Look for a clause that opens with a word that makes it wait for more.

questions.prompt: Julius Caesar's report of his victory, in the English version, runs “I came, I saw, I conquered.” How many of its parts begin with “I”?
hints: Split the line at each comma.
Look at the first word of each part.
Count the parts that open with the same word.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: each of the three short parts begins with “I”.

questions.onCorrect: Three: each of the three short parts begins with “I”, so the line is both a tricolon and an example of anaphora.

misconceptions.feedback: Split the line at each comma and look at the first word of every part.
Only the first part is easy to notice. Check how the other two parts begin.

questions.prompt: In “Every day, every hour, every minute”, which word repeats at the start of each part?
hints: Compare the first word of each part.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: every

questions.onCorrect: “Every” opens each part. Repeating the opening word is anaphora, and it draws the eye to what changes.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the parts that change. Find the word that stays the same each time.

questions.prompt: “Never let a fool kiss you or a kiss fool you.” In the second half, which of the two repeated words comes first?
hints: Compare the two halves. Which word leads in each?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: kiss

questions.onCorrect: “Kiss” comes first in the second half, “fool” in the first. The terms return in reverse order: chiasmus.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the order of the first half. In the second half the order flips.

questions.prompt: Which line is built as an antithesis?
hints: Look for opposed ideas placed in parallel form.

acceptedIdeas: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”

choices.label: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”
“Fair is foul, and foul is fair.”

questions.onCorrect: “To err is human; to forgive, divine” sets human error against divine forgiveness in two parallel halves.

misconceptions.feedback: That line is a series of three parallel actions, which makes it a tricolon, and nothing in it is set against anything else.
The two halves of that line swap the same two words, so the figure is a chiasmus rather than an antithesis.

questions.prompt: Your friend watches the rain soak her picnic and says “Wonderful weather.” What does she mean?
hints: What has just happened to her picnic?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She means the opposite of what she says.

questions.onCorrect: She means the opposite of what she says. The soaked picnic is the context that tells you the words are not meant at face value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the words say, but look at what has just happened to the picnic. The context points the other way.
Nothing in her words or in the scene is about change. She is reacting to the rain that has ruined her picnic.

questions.prompt: A friend says “Nice parking” about a car wedged across two bays. Which word means the opposite of what she thinks?
hints: Which word praises something she does not praise?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: nice

questions.onCorrect: “Nice” says the opposite of her view. The gap is plain because everyone can see the car.

misconceptions.feedback: “Parking” is accurate. Find the word whose meaning she reverses.

questions.prompt: Which of these is not dramatic irony?
hints: Ask of each statement who knows what.
Dramatic irony needs the audience to know more than a character.
One statement is about an unexpected outcome, not about knowledge.

acceptedIdeas: A bakery runs out of bread on its opening day.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bakery runs out of bread on its opening day.

choices.label: A bakery runs out of bread on its opening day.
The audience sees the villain pocket the key as the hero says “I trust you.”
The audience knows the letter is forged, but the heroine does not.

questions.onCorrect: The bakery's empty shelves are an outcome that reverses what an opening day should bring, which makes it situational irony. In the other two the audience knows what a character does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The audience knows the letter is forged and the heroine does not, and that gap in knowledge is what makes dramatic irony.
The audience has seen the villain take the key while the hero trusts him, so the audience knows more than the hero, which is dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: A fire station burns to the ground. What kind of irony is that: verbal, dramatic or situational?
hints: Does anyone say or know anything here, or does an event simply turn out oddly?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: situational

questions.onCorrect: Situational irony: the building meant to fight fires is destroyed by one, so the outcome turns against its purpose. No one has said anything or known anything in advance.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody speaks here, so there is no statement to mean its opposite. The irony lies in the event itself.
Dramatic irony needs an audience that knows more than a character. This is simply an event that turns out against its own purpose.

questions.prompt: A text message reads “We waited, the bus never came”. Could each half stand as a sentence by itself?
hints: Put a full stop after each half and read it on its own.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both halves could

choices.label: Neither could, since each needs the other

questions.onCorrect: Each half has a subject and a finite verb and makes sense alone, which is exactly why a comma by itself is too light to hold them together.

misconceptions.feedback: “The bus never came” has its own subject, the bus, and its own finite verb, so it could end with a full stop as well.
“We waited” is short, but it has a subject and a finite verb and says something complete, so it could be a sentence.
Each half makes sense with a full stop after it. The two are related in meaning, but neither depends on the other grammatically.

questions.prompt: Which mark links two clauses as one thought, without a conjunction?
hints: Think of the mark that sits between a comma and a full stop in strength.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: semicolon

questions.onCorrect: A semicolon links two full clauses as one thought and leaves their relation unstated.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma on its own is too weak to hold two full clauses.
A full stop keeps the clauses apart. The question asks for a mark that links them.

questions.prompt: Why does the semicolon need no conjunction here?

acceptedIdeas: It already links two full clauses as one thought.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon links two complete clauses without a conjunction.

choices.label: It is just a heavier comma.
It already links two full clauses as one thought.

questions.onCorrect: A semicolon is a full link between clauses: it joins them without saying how they relate.

misconceptions.feedback: A comma cannot do this job, so the semicolon is not just a stronger version of it.
Semicolons do separate list items that contain commas, but they also join clauses.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
hints: Check that each side of the semicolon could stand as a sentence.

acceptedIdeas: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.

choices.label: The match was cancelled; the pitch was flooded.
The match was cancelled; because the pitch was flooded.

questions.onCorrect: Each side of the semicolon is a complete clause, and the semicolon asks no conjunction to join them.

misconceptions.feedback: “Because the pitch was flooded” is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone, so it cannot sit after a semicolon.
“Although the match” is not a complete clause, and a semicolon needs a complete clause on each side.

questions.prompt: Clap along to “Twinkle, twinkle, little star”, once on each beat. How many claps do you make?
hints: Say the line aloud and tap along.
Tap harder on the strong syllables.
Count only the strong taps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR, one on each stressed syllable.

questions.onCorrect: Four: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR, one clap on each stressed syllable. The syllables between the claps are the weak ones.

misconceptions.feedback: Seven is the number of syllables. A clap falls only on the strong ones, so you clap less often than you speak.
Say the line aloud again and tap harder on the strong syllables. The last word is strong too.

questions.prompt: “com-PARE” is an iamb. Does its beat fall on the first or the second syllable?
hints: Say “compare” and listen for the louder syllable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: second

questions.onCorrect: The beat falls on the second syllable. An iamb is a weak syllable followed by a strong one.

misconceptions.feedback: Say the word aloud. The strong syllable is the later one.

questions.prompt: Why does “They also serve who only stand and waite” count as iambic pentameter?

acceptedIdeas: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.

choices.label: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.

questions.onCorrect: Five iambs make ten syllables, with the beats on every second one.

misconceptions.feedback: The line has eight words, and words are not what the metre counts. Count syllables and pairs.
Several words have two syllables. Metre counts the pattern of weak and strong.

questions.prompt: Which line has an extra unstressed syllable after its last beat?
hints: Count the syllables in each line. Which has one too many?

acceptedIdeas: To be, or not to be, that is the question
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To be, or not to be, that is the question

choices.label: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
They also serve who only stand and waite
To be, or not to be, that is the question

questions.onCorrect: “To be, or not to be, that is the question” has eleven syllables, and the last, “-tion”, is a weak syllable after the final beat on “ques-”. That is a feminine ending.

misconceptions.feedback: That line has ten syllables, and its last syllable, “day”, is the final beat. Nothing follows the last beat.
That line has ten syllables and ends on a beat, so it has no extra syllable after the last beat.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in a regular line of iambic tetrameter?
hints: How many feet does tetrameter have?
How many syllables does an iamb have?
Multiply the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four iambs of two syllables each make eight.

questions.onCorrect: Eight: tetrameter has four feet, and each iamb holds two syllables.

misconceptions.feedback: Ten syllables belong to pentameter, which has five feet. Tetrameter has one foot fewer.
Four is the number of feet. Each iamb has two syllables, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A friend retells her day: “I walked in and everyone went quiet.” Where is she in relation to the story?
hints: Who does the word “I” point to?

acceptedIdeas: She is a character in it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She says “I”, so she is a character in it.

choices.label: She is a character in it.

questions.onCorrect: She says “I”, so she is inside the story she tells. Where the narrator stands changes what we learn.

misconceptions.feedback: She says “I” and describes her own entrance, so she is part of the events.
She is the one telling it. Ask who the “I” is.

questions.prompt: A narrator says “we trudged home”. Is that first, second or third person?
hints: Is the narrator one of the people described?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: first

questions.onCorrect: “We” includes the narrator, so the narration is in the first person.

misconceptions.feedback: Third person calls the characters “he”, “she” or “they”. This narrator is among the “we”.
Second person addresses the reader as “you”. Who is the “we”?

questions.prompt: In free indirect discourse, whose grammatical person and tense does the sentence use: the narrator's or the character's?
hints: Compare it with direct speech, which uses the character's own person.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: narrator

questions.onCorrect: The sentence keeps the narrator's person and tense, while the character's words and feeling show through.

misconceptions.feedback: The character's own words would be direct speech, which keeps their own person and tense.

questions.prompt: Why is “What a dreadful day it had been!” free indirect discourse and not plain narration?

acceptedIdeas: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.

choices.label: It keeps Anna's own exclamation inside the narrator's grammar.
It is in the first person.

questions.onCorrect: Third person and past tense come from the narrator, while the exclamation is Anna's own.

misconceptions.feedback: Quotation marks would make it direct speech. This sentence has none.
It says “it had been”, so the narrator's third person and past tense remain.

questions.prompt: Turn Tom's direct thought “I am so tired!” into free indirect discourse. Which two words replace “I am”?
hints: The narrator speaks about Tom, not as Tom.
Both the person and the tense shift.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: he was

questions.onCorrect: “He was so tired!” keeps Tom's exclamation, but the person changes to the third and the tense moves back to the past.

misconceptions.feedback: The person is right, but free indirect discourse also moves the verb into the narrator's past tense.
The narrator speaks about Tom and not as Tom, so both the person and the tense change.

questions.prompt: “Roses are red / Violets are blue / Sugar is sweet / And so are you.” Which line number rhymes with line 2?
hints: Say the last word of each line.
Which ending sounds like “blue”?
Give that line's number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 4: “blue” and “you” rhyme.

questions.onCorrect: Line 4: “blue” and “you” rhyme, so lines 2 and 4 share a sound. Lines 1 and 3 end on different sounds, so the scheme is ABCB.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 1 ends on “red”, which does not sound like “blue”. Say the last word of each line and listen for the one that does.
Line 3 ends on “sweet”. Compare its sound with “blue” and then with the last line.

questions.prompt: A quatrain rhymes ABAB. Which line number rhymes with line 1?
hints: Each letter stands for one rhyme sound.
Which lines carry the letter A?
Give the line that is not line 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Line 3: the letter A appears on lines 1 and 3.

questions.onCorrect: Line 3. Each letter is one rhyme sound, and lines that share a letter rhyme.

misconceptions.feedback: Line 2 is B. Look for the other line marked A.
Line 4 is B. Look for the other line marked A.
Line 1 is the line you are matching. Find the other one.

questions.prompt: In a Petrarchan sonnet, after which line does the volta usually fall?
hints: How long is the octave?
The turn comes where the octave gives way to the sestet.
Count the lines of the octave.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After line 8, where the octave gives way to the sestet.

questions.onCorrect: After line 8: the octave sets out the problem and the sestet answers it.

misconceptions.feedback: The sestet has six lines. The turn comes where the octave ends.
That is the last line of the poem. Find where the first part ends.
That ends the first quatrain. In this form the first part is longer.

questions.prompt: A Petrarchan sestet rhymes CDECDE. How many different rhyme sounds does it use?
hints: Each letter is one rhyme sound.
Ignore repeats of a letter.
Count the distinct letters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: C, D and E.

questions.onCorrect: Three: C, D and E. Each is used twice in the six lines.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is the number of lines. A letter stands for a sound that is used on more than one line.
Look again at the scheme: CDECDE has a third letter that is neither C nor D.

questions.prompt: Say “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” How many words begin with the p sound?
hints: Say it aloud and listen to how each word begins.
Ignore the small words in between.
Count the words that start with the p sound.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: Peter, Piper, picked, peck, pickled and peppers.

questions.onCorrect: Six: Peter, Piper, picked, peck, pickled and peppers. “Of” and “a” are small words that do not begin with the sound.

misconceptions.feedback: You may have counted “of”, which begins with a vowel sound. Say each word aloud and listen only to its first sound.
One of the p words has been missed. Say the line slowly and tap on each word that starts with the sound.

questions.prompt: How many of these pairs alliterate: knee and nose; cat and city; phone and fish?
hints: Say each pair aloud.
Listen for the first sound, not the first letter.
“Phone” and “fish” begin the same way, but check the others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: knee and nose share the n sound, and phone and fish share the f sound. Cat and city start with k and s.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Alliteration follows sound, not spelling: knee and nose match, and so do phone and fish.

misconceptions.feedback: Say each pair aloud. Spelling can mislead you in both directions.
Say “cat” and “city” aloud. Do they begin with the same sound?
Listen to the first sound of each word, not its first letter.

questions.prompt: Which word marks the comparison in “Her voice was like honey”?
hints: Which small word says that two things are being compared?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: like

questions.onCorrect: “Like” announces the comparison. That makes it a simile, and without it the line would be a metaphor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the thing she is compared with. Find the small word that announces the comparison.
That is what is being described. Find the word that announces the comparison.

questions.prompt: In Wordsworth's “I wandered lonely as a Cloud”, which is the vehicle?
hints: Which word names the thing borrowed to make a picture?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: a Cloud

questions.onCorrect: The vehicle is the cloud, the picture borrowed to describe the speaker. The speaker, “I”, is the tenor.

misconceptions.feedback: “I” is the thing being described, which is the tenor. The vehicle is the image used to describe it.
“Lonely” names the quality being shown. The vehicle is the thing borrowed to show it.

questions.prompt: A film's tension in five scenes runs 1, 3, 6, 9, 5. Which scene is the tensest?
hints: Read the five numbers in order.
Which number is the largest?
Give that number's place in the list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Scene 4: its tension of 9 is the highest.

questions.onCorrect: Scene 4: its tension of 9 is the highest, and the tension falls away after it. A story's high point is the scene where the line stops rising.

misconceptions.feedback: Nine is the tension of that scene, not its place in the list. The question asks for the scene number.
Scene 3 has tension 6, which is still rising. Look for the scene after which the numbers start to fall.
Scene 5 is the last scene, but its tension has already dropped to 5. The tensest scene is the one with the largest number.

questions.prompt: At which part of Freytag's pyramid do the protagonist's fortunes stop rising and start to fall?
hints: Think of the peak of the pyramid.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: climax

questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point of the pyramid. Before it fortunes rise, and after it they fall.

misconceptions.feedback: The rise leads up to that point. Name the point itself.
Those come after the high point. Name the point where the turn happens.

questions.prompt: A story's three scenes run: + to −, − to +, + to +. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and the second change value. The third opens and closes at +.

questions.onCorrect: Two: the first goes from + to − and the second from − to +. The third opens and closes on +, so it holds its value.

misconceptions.feedback: A scene turns only when its closing sign differs from its opening sign. Check the third scene again.
Compare the opening and closing sign of each scene in turn. More than one of them differs.

questions.prompt: Another story's four scenes run: − to +, + to +, + to −, − to −. How many of them turn?
hints: Write each scene's opening sign and closing sign.
A scene turns when the two signs differ.
Count the scenes whose signs differ.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the first and third change value.

questions.onCorrect: Two: the first goes from − to + and the third from + to −. The second and fourth open and close on the same sign.

misconceptions.feedback: A scene turns only when its two signs differ. Two of these scenes keep the same sign from start to end.
Check the second and fourth scenes again: each opens and closes on the same sign.

questions.prompt: Why is scene 3 the climax rather than scene 6?

acceptedIdeas: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall afterwards.

choices.label: Fortunes rise until scene 3 and fall after it.

questions.onCorrect: The climax is the highest point: the story builds up to it and falls away afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: Position is not the test. Ask where the heights stop rising.
Nothing here measures how long a scene lasts. Look at the heights.

questions.prompt: In “The storm was fierce”, what does “fierce” do?
hints: Ask whether anything in the clause is having something done to it.
Try removing the word: does “The storm was” still say anything?

acceptedIdeas: It says what the subject is like.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It says what the subject is like.

choices.label: It says what the subject is like.
It says when the storm happened.
It receives the action of the verb.

questions.onCorrect: “Was” links the storm to a description, and “fierce” completes that link. That is a complement's job, whereas an object has to receive an action.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing is being done to anything in this clause. “Was” does not describe an action, so there is no object to receive one.
A word that says when would be a modifier, and the clause would survive without it. Here the clause is unfinished without “fierce”.

questions.prompt: Which repair says outright that the room went dark because the lamp flickered?
hints: Which repair puts a word of cause between the clauses?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A comma followed by “so”

choices.label: A full stop between the clauses

questions.onCorrect: “So” names the relation, a result. The semicolon and the full stop leave the reader to infer it.

misconceptions.feedback: A semicolon only shows that the two clauses belong together. The reader has to work out for themselves whether one caused the other.
A full stop separates the thoughts and says nothing about how they connect.

questions.prompt: In “The report was approved by the director in May”, which phrase holds the actor?
hints: Ask who did the approving.
In a passive sentence the doer follows the word “by”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “by the director”

questions.onCorrect: The director did the approving, and the passive pushes the doer to the end behind “by”.

misconceptions.feedback: “Was approved” is the verb. It tells you what happened to the report but not who did it.
“In May” says when, so it is a modifier. The doer is whoever approved the report.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the unstated rule that links the forecast to the claim?
hints: The claim is “It will rain tomorrow”, and the grounds are the forecast. What must you believe for one to support the other?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Forecasts are usually right.

choices.label: The forecast was published this morning.

questions.onCorrect: Without the belief that forecasts are usually right, a forecast would give no reason to expect rain. That general rule is the warrant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the claim itself, the statement the argument is trying to establish. The warrant is a general rule behind it.
That is one more particular fact about the forecast. A warrant is a general rule, not another fact.

questions.prompt: What job does “As a lifelong farmer” do in the speaker's sentence?
hints: Ask whether the clause is about the policy or about the person speaking.

acceptedIdeas: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.

choices.label: It builds trust in the speaker's experience.
It gives a reason for the policy.

questions.onCorrect: The clause tells us who is speaking and for how long, so it asks the audience to trust the speaker's experience. That is the work of ethos.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the clause frightens anyone. It simply tells us who is speaking.
The clause gives no reason for or against a policy. It is about the speaker, and that is the mark of ethos.

questions.prompt: Counting from the first syllable of “They also serve who only stand and wait”, which syllable carries the beat on “stand”?
hints: Number the syllables in order: “they” is 1, “al” is 2, “so” is 3.
Keep counting through “who only” until you reach “stand”.
An iamb puts its beat on an even-numbered syllable, so the answer should be even.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Syllable 8: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand, so “stand” is the eighth, an even-numbered place where an iamb puts its beat.

questions.onCorrect: The five strong syllables fall on 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, so the line is five iambs, a regular line of iambic pentameter.

misconceptions.feedback: Seven takes you to “ly”, the weak half of “only”. The beat on “stand” comes one syllable later.
“Stand” carries the fourth beat, but the question asks which syllable of the line it is, and each beat has a weak syllable before it.

questions.prompt: What does “What a dreadful day it had been!” keep from Anna's own thought?
hints: Compare the sentence with her direct thought, “What a dreadful day it has been!”
Ask which of the three things listed is still on the page.

acceptedIdeas: Her exclamation, inside the narrator's grammar.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Her exclamation, inside the narrator's grammar.

choices.label: Her exclamation, inside the narrator's grammar.

questions.onCorrect: The exclamation is Anna's own, but it is set in the narrator's past tense, so the sentence is both her voice and the narrator's grammar.

misconceptions.feedback: There are no quotation marks, and that is part of what makes the sentence free indirect. Without them the thought merges into the narration.
The sentence contains no “I”. It stays in the narrator's grammar and keeps only the character's exclamation.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities (1859): “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.” Which description fits the way these clauses are built?
hints: Look at what stays the same at the start of each clause, and at what changes.

acceptedIdeas: It holds the opening still, so that the changing endings stand out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It holds the opening still, so that the changing endings stand out

choices.label: It holds the opening still, so that the changing endings stand out
It reverses the order of the key words in each half
It makes a set of three parallel members

questions.onCorrect: The repeated opening is anaphora, and Dickens keeps it going for ten clauses in the full sentence, so each new ending lands against the same frame.

misconceptions.feedback: No words swap places: every clause starts with “it was” in the same order, and only the ending changes.
The extract has four clauses, not three, and what ties them together is their shared opening.

questions.prompt: Julius Caesar's report of his victory, in the English version, runs “I came, I saw, I conquered.” Which two figures does it combine?
hints: Ask what is repeated and what changes.
Count the clauses, then look at how each one begins.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tricolon and anaphora

questions.onCorrect: Three short clauses alike in form make a tricolon, and the “I” that opens each of them is anaphora, so the line is both at once.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing returns in reverse order and nothing is set against its opposite; the three clauses run forward in the same shape.
The clauses do open the same way, which is anaphora, but coming, seeing and conquering are not opposed, so there is no antithesis.
The three clauses do make a tricolon, but no terms come back in reverse order, so there is no chiasmus.

questions.prompt: Say “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.” What does the line repeat?
hints: Say the line slowly and listen to how each word begins.

acceptedIdeas: The consonant sound that opens the words
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The consonant sound that opens the words

choices.label: A vowel sound inside the words
The same word at the start of each clause
The consonant sound that opens the words

questions.onCorrect: Six of its eight words open on the p sound, and repeating the opening consonant sound of nearby words is alliteration.

misconceptions.feedback: The vowels change from word to word, from the long e of “Peter” to the short i of “picked”; what stays the same is the sound each word starts with.
No word is repeated; the words are all different, and what most of them share is their first sound.

questions.prompt: In his funeral speech Antony calls Brutus “an honourable man” again and again, each time beside a fact that tells in Caesar's favour. What does the repetition do?
hints: Look at what each repetition of the phrase is placed next to.

acceptedIdeas: It makes the praise sound hollow, so the crowd hears an accusation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes the praise sound hollow, so the crowd hears an accusation

choices.label: It makes the praise sound hollow, so the crowd hears an accusation
It shows that Antony has come to admire Brutus
It defends Brutus sincerely against the crowd's anger

questions.onCorrect: The words stay the same while the evidence against Brutus's charge of ambition grows, so each repetition sounds less like praise, and the crowd ends up hearing the opposite of what is said.

misconceptions.feedback: Each time the phrase sits beside a fact showing that Caesar was not ambitious, which is what Brutus claimed, so the praise and the facts pull apart.
On the surface the words defend Brutus, but Antony sets them beside the evidence against him, and by the end of the scene the crowd is calling for the conspirators' blood.

flashcards.front: In 'Thou art more lovely and more temperate', what grammatical function does 'more lovely and more temperate' serve after the linking verb 'art'?
flashcards.back: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A subject complement: after a linking verb it describes the subject, 'thou'.

flashcards.front: How many finite verbs are in 'When I consider how my light is spent, I fondly ask'? Count 'is spent' as one verb.
flashcards.back: Three: 'consider', 'is spent' and 'ask'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three: 'consider', 'is spent' and 'ask'.

flashcards.front: Which mark joins two independent clauses in one sentence without a conjunction and leaves their relation unstated?
flashcards.back: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.

flashcards.front: What must the words before a colon form?
flashcards.back: A complete (independent) clause. 'The reasons were: cost and delay' fails this test.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A complete (independent) clause. 'The reasons were: cost and delay' fails this test.

flashcards.front: Unbury the verb in 'We had a discussion about the budget' to get 'We discussed the budget'. How many words are saved?
flashcards.back: Seven words become four; three are saved.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven words become four; three are saved.

flashcards.front: In 'The window was broken', which participant in the action has the passive left out?
flashcards.back: The agent, or actor: the sentence never says who broke the window.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The agent, or actor: the sentence never says who broke the window.

flashcards.front: In Toulmin's model, which element limits the force of a claim with words such as 'probably' or 'in most cases'?
flashcards.back: The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.

flashcards.front: Which Toulmin element states the conditions under which a claim would not hold?
flashcards.back: The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.

flashcards.front: How many years is 'four score and seven'?
flashcards.back: Four twenties make eighty; add seven.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four twenties make eighty; add seven.

flashcards.front: Which of Aristotle's three appeals works through the emotions of the audience?
flashcards.back: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pathos: persuasion through the feelings a speech arouses.

flashcards.front: 'We do not live to eat; we eat to live.' Name the figure that reverses the order of the repeated words.
flashcards.back: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Chiasmus, or more strictly antimetabole: live, eat / eat, live.

flashcards.front: What is a series of three parallel members, as in 'I came, I saw, I conquered', called?
flashcards.back: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tricolon: three parallel members, here three short clauses.

flashcards.front: How many syllables are in Milton's 'They also serve who only stand and waite'?
flashcards.back: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: they / al / so / serve / who / on / ly / stand / and / waite. A regular iambic pentameter line.

flashcards.front: Name the metrical foot with the pattern unstressed then stressed.
flashcards.back: The iamb, as in 'com-PARE'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The iamb, as in 'com-PARE'.

flashcards.front: How many words in Keats's 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' begin with the m sound?
flashcards.back: Two: 'mists' and 'mellow'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: 'mists' and 'mellow'.

flashcards.front: In I. A. Richards's terms, what is the subject a metaphor describes called, as opposed to its vehicle?
flashcards.back: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tenor. In 'Juliet is the sun', Juliet is the tenor and the sun the vehicle.

flashcards.front: How many lines are in the sestet of a Petrarchan sonnet?
flashcards.back: Six; the octave has eight.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six; the octave has eight.

flashcards.front: What is the Italian term for the turn in a sonnet's argument?
flashcards.back: The volta: the point where the argument changes direction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The volta: the point where the argument changes direction.

flashcards.front: In which grammatical person does a narrator write who is also a character and says 'I'?
flashcards.back: First person: the narrator is inside the story and says 'I'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: First person: the narrator is inside the story and says 'I'.

flashcards.front: What does free indirect discourse leave out that indirect speech such as 'she thought that it was hopeless' includes?
flashcards.back: The reporting verb (the reporting clause 'she thought that').

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reporting verb (the reporting clause 'she thought that').

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what is meant?
flashcards.back: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Verbal irony: the words say one thing and mean another.

flashcards.front: Which kind of irony arises when an outcome reverses the intention that produced it?
flashcards.back: Situational irony: events turn against the purpose that set them going.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Situational irony: events turn against the purpose that set them going.

flashcards.front: A story's five scenes run: + to +, + to −, − to −, − to +, + to +. How many scenes turn?
flashcards.back: Two: the second (+ to −) and the fourth (− to +).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the second (+ to −) and the fourth (− to +).

flashcards.front: Name the part of Freytag's pyramid between the climax and the catastrophe.
flashcards.back: The falling action, which Freytag calls the return or fall.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The falling action, which Freytag calls the return or fall.

citations.claim: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation, as in Sonnet 18, lines 2 and 3.
The words before a colon must form a complete clause.
Conjunctions name a relation, semicolons leave it unstated, colons explain, and dashes break the sentence for emphasis.
Independent clauses are counted by their subjects and finite verbs, whatever mark joins them.
A splice is repaired by keeping the comma and adding a coordinating conjunction such as “so”.
It is called a comma splice, from the sense of splicing two lengths of rope end to end, with the comma as the weak join.
Each side of the semicolon is a complete clause, and the semicolon asks no conjunction to join them.
The verb is “is”: your boasted liberty is an unholy license, and the semicolon marks the place where the repeated verb has been dropped.
The words before the colon, “The verdict was clear”, form a complete clause, and what follows explains them. A colon needs that complete clause in front of it.
“So” joins the two clauses and states that leaving was the result of the lateness: “It was late, so we left.”
“But” (or “yet”) keeps the contrast and repairs the splice: “You may rejoice, but I must mourn.” “And” would flatten the opposition.
There are three: “The hall was full”, “the speaker was late” and “his train had stopped outside the city”. The semicolon and the colon each join complete clauses.
Each half has a subject and a finite verb and makes sense alone, which is exactly why a comma by itself is too light to hold them together.
“So” names the relation, a result. The semicolon and the full stop leave the reader to infer it.
A semicolon. A colon would claim that the second clause explains the first.
A complete (independent) clause. 'The reasons were: cost and delay' fails this test.
In the active voice the subject performs the action; in the passive it receives it and the actor moves behind “by”.
Turning “The window was broken by Sam” into the active gives “Sam broke the window”.
A passive may omit its agent, which is why it can hide who is responsible.
The agent of a passive sits in a “by” phrase and becomes the subject of the active version.
“Mistakes were made by the finance office” becomes “The finance office made mistakes”.
“The motion was rejected by the committee” becomes “The committee rejected the motion”, two words shorter.
Nominalisation turns a verb into a noun, hiding the action behind a weak verb.
Replacing “made a decision” with “decided” and “conduct a review of” with “review” saves five words.
Framing phrases and redundant modifiers can be cut without loss of meaning.

citations.claim: A Toulmin argument has a claim, the statement to be accepted, and grounds, the facts offered for it.
The claim is identified by asking which statement the others are offered to support, not by its position.
The warrant is the usually unstated general rule that licenses the step from grounds to claim.
Advice such as “Get a dog: mine makes me happy” leaves its warrant unstated.
A warrant such as “forecasts are usually right” links the grounds to the claim.
“Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it” is the warrant linking the grounds to the claim.
An opponent can leave the grounds alone and challenge the warrant.
A qualifier limits the force of a claim and a rebuttal states the conditions under which it would not hold.
“Probably” is the qualifier in “Harriet will probably win”.
Backing is support for the warrant itself, as distinct from grounds, which support the claim.
Sorting statements into claim, grounds, warrant and rebuttal identifies the warrant as the general rule.
“The bridge should close to lorries” is what the writer wants you to accept, and the other two statements exist to support it.
“Unless the pitch floods” names a condition under which the claim would fail, and that is what a rebuttal does.
It is the warrant, the general rule that allows the move from these grounds to this claim.
“Probably” says how strongly the claim is made, while “unless rain keeps her supporters at home” gives the condition under which it fails.
It is a general rule that links the fall in sales, the grounds, to the conclusion about price, the claim. The “unless” statement is the rebuttal.
The doubled attendance is the observed fact offered as a reason, so it is the grounds. The opening late is the claim, the rule about staffing cost the warrant, and the short trial a rebuttal.
Support for the warrant itself is called backing. Grounds support the claim, whereas backing stands behind the rule that links them.
She states the claim and the grounds aloud and leaves the rule that links them for you to supply, and that unstated rule is the part worth questioning.
Without the belief that forecasts are usually right, a forecast would give no reason to expect rain. That general rule is the warrant.
The qualifier: it states how strongly the claim is made.
The rebuttal, sometimes called the reservation.
